slides.title: A popular database, the wrong job
slides.tldr: Pick a database by how your data will be written and queried, not by what is trendy right now.

blocks.body: Ryan picked a document database for a new e-commerce project because everyone on YouTube said "it's modern, no schema needed". The first month went fast. Six months later the finance team wanted a sales report by state, and payments needed to change an order, the stock and a payment balance together. In a relational database both of those are a single statement. Ryan had to build them by hand in his own code.

blocks.caption: The same decision: how it felt in month one, and what it became six months later

columns.title: In month one
items: No tables to create, save whatever you like
One order = one JSON, easy to read
No migrations to write
columns.tip: At the start there is little data and the questions are simple, so any database feels fine. A wrong choice stays hidden.

columns.title: Six months later
items: A report means stitching five collections together in code
The same customer's name is spelled three ways in three places
An order was placed but stock never dropped: it broke halfway
Old documents lack the new field, so the code is full of ifs
columns.tip: The data was interlinked (order, product, customer) and the questions needed joins. The wrong kind of notebook had been chosen for the job.

blocks.body: Choose a database by its access patterns, not by its popularity.

items.meaning: The list of how your app will write data and how it will look it up.
The fixed shape of the data: which columns each table has and which are required.
Combining rows from two tables by matching a shared column.

items.label: Why choosing a database is a pillar decision

check.q: What exactly was Ryan's mistake? Is a document database a bad thing?
check.a: No, it is not bad. The mistake was how he chose: his data was interlinked and his questions needed joins and transactions, which is relational territory. He chose by popularity instead of looking at the work.

slides.title: Six kinds of databases, six kinds of notebooks
slides.tldr: Relational, document, key-value, wide-column, graph and time-series: each is built for a different kind of question.

blocks.title: Six notebooks in a hospital
blocks.body: A hospital does not keep all its information in one kind of notebook. Admissions and bills go in a ruled register, each patient's papers go in their own file, and a chart at the bedside gets the temperature written in every hour. One question decides the kind of notebook: **how will this information be looked up later?** The six database families split along exactly the same line.

blocks.caption: The six families: what the data looks like, what each is best at, and what you give up

cells: Easy spreading of writes over many servers
rows.tip: Tables, rows and columns, linked by IDs. Even questions nobody planned for can be asked in SQL, which makes this the most versatile family. The price: one main server takes all the writes, so growth past it needs real work.

cells: Data read and written as one whole
Joins across documents: you build them in code
rows.tip: One JSON document holds everything about one thing. Documents can differ in shape, but joins and multi-document transactions are weak.

cells: A key and one opaque value
Very fast get and set by key
Searching or filtering by what is inside
rows.tip: You get the value only if you know the key. You cannot say "give me all the red reports". Ideal for caches, sessions and counters.

cells: Rows grouped by a partition key
Joins and questions you did not plan
rows.tip: Data is spread across many servers by partition key. Writes are very fast, but you decide the queries first and shape the tables around them. There are no joins.

cells: Cheap totals and reports over everything
rows.tip: Built from nodes and edges. A "friend of a friend of a friend" question becomes a deep join in SQL; here it is the natural operation.
Each row is a timestamp plus a measurement. Data is only appended, never edited, and queries ask about time windows, like "the average over the last hour".

aside.body: The kind of question picks the kind of notebook. Write down the questions first, then choose.

items: The family borders are not rigid: PostgreSQL has JSON columns, Redis has lists and sorted sets, and DynamoDB sits between key-value and wide-column.
A search engine (Elasticsearch) is yet another family, covered in the [[caching/search-basics/like-fails|search section]].

check.q: Server CPU readings arriving every second, and "who follows whom": which family fits each?
check.a: CPU readings arrive over time and are only appended: time-series. The follow network is about walking relationships: graph (though at a small scale relational does the job fine).

slides.title: Write the access patterns first
slides.tldr: On one page, list what the app will do with data, how often, and with what guarantees. The database name falls out of it.

blocks.body: Before you think of a database name, write one page on what the app will actually do with its data. Next to each job, note three things: what the job is, how often it runs, and what you need from the database. Below is the page for an e-commerce app. Notice how most of the lines point the same way.

blocks.code:
Job 1  Create an order: changes order + stock + payment together
       50/second     need: transaction, constraints
Job 2  "My orders" list, newest first
       300/second    need: lookup by customer_id, sorted result
Job 3  Monthly sales report by state
       20 per day    need: join + GROUP BY
Job 4  Search products by name
       200/second    need: full-text search
Job 5  Login session
       1000/second   need: read by key, expiry (TTL)

Decision
Jobs 1-3  ->  PostgreSQL (main data, source of truth)
Job 4     ->  PostgreSQL full-text for now; a search engine only if measured slow
Job 5     ->  Redis (key-value)

marks.tip: Changing three places together while keeping the rules intact: this one line already says the main database must be relational.
Report questions are not known in advance and keep changing. SQL gives you the freedom to ask anything.
Try the database you already have before adding a new one. The next step comes only after you have measured it slow.

blocks.caption: From the page to a decision in four steps

steps.title: 1. List the jobs
steps.body: The app's main 5 to 10 reads and writes, in plain words.
steps.tip: Not every job, only the ones that run most often or hurt most when they go wrong.

steps.title: 2. List the needs
steps.body: Beside each: how often, and what you need: transaction, join, key lookup, TTL.
steps.tip: If you do not know exact numbers, guess. Knowing whether it is 10 or 10 thousand is enough.

steps.title: 3. Pick the main database
steps.body: Whichever way most jobs point is your source of truth.
steps.tip: For almost every business app this answer is relational, because the data is linked and money needs transactions.

steps.title: 4. Split off the misfits
steps.body: Only for a job that does not fit the main database, consider a second one.
steps.tip: Temporary, key-based jobs such as sessions or caches are usually the first misfits, which is why Redis is so often the second database.

items: How to estimate the numbers is covered in [[thinking/estimation/wedding-rice|back-of-the-envelope maths]].
This same page later becomes the evidence in your design doc for "why this database".

items.meaning: The database whose data is treated as final; everything elsewhere is a copy of it.
Time to live: how long until the data deletes itself.

check.q: Which three things do you write beside each job on an access-pattern page?
check.a: What the job is (read or write, by which key or condition), how often it runs, and what you need from the database, such as a transaction, a join, sorted results or a TTL.

slides.title: When in doubt, go relational
slides.tldr: Most business data is linked, so the default is PostgreSQL or MySQL; the shapeless part can go in a JSON column.

blocks.body: Most business data is interlinked: a customer's orders, an order's payments. For this kind of data a relational database gives you three things ready-made: transactions, constraints, and SQL for any question you think of later. And "some of our data has no fixed shape" is no reason for a separate document database, because both PostgreSQL and MySQL have JSON columns.

marks.tip: Anything every row has, and anything you calculate or enforce rules on, is always a plain column, with NOT NULL and the right type.
On PostgreSQL this becomes a JSONB column; on MySQL it is plain JSON. Before DBAL 4.3 you wrote Types::JSON with the option jsonb => true.
A GIN index speeds up lookups by the keys and values inside the JSON. You just got the main benefit of a document database.

blocks.body: When in doubt, start relational. Bring in another database only when you can measure the pain.

use: The data is linked and the future questions are not fully known yet
Money, stock, bookings: anywhere that cannot live without transactions and constraints
avoid: Hundreds of thousands of writes per second, more than one server can take
Temporary data read only by key, such as a cache or sessions

items.label: What a transaction actually gives you
How to lay out your tables

check.q: Products need different attributes per product. Is that alone a reason to adopt a document database?
check.a: No. A relational database can hold them in a JSON column, and you can index it. Fixed facts like name and price stay in ordinary columns, with constraints.

slides.title: A second database: when, and at what price
slides.tldr: Every new database means new backups, monitoring and syncing work; keep the truth in one place and make the rest copies of it.

blocks.body: Adding a database is not just installing a library. It brings its own backups, monitoring, upgrades and 3 a.m. incidents, and they all land on your team. The hardest part is that the same fact now lives in two places, and you own keeping them in agreement. So the rule is: the truth lives in **one** place, and everything else is a copy that can be deleted and rebuilt.

blocks.caption: One source of truth, everything else a copy of it

nodes.label: Symfony app
nodes.tip: The app sends every durable write to one place only. It never writes a "main" copy to two databases side by side.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.tip: Orders, money, users: the final truth is here. If anything elsewhere disagrees, this one is right.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.tip: Answers needed again and again, plus sessions, with an expiry. Even if all of it vanishes you lose nothing, things are just slow for a while.

nodes.label: Messenger worker
nodes.tip: Copies changes from the main database to other places in the background, and retries if it fails.

nodes.label: Search index
nodes.tip: A separately arranged copy for fast lookup by product name. It may lag by a few seconds.

edges.label: Every write goes to PostgreSQL first: that is the truth
Answers read again and again, and sessions, are kept in Redis with an expiry
News of the change travels to the worker as a message
The worker copies that change into the search index
If the index is lost, it can be rebuilt entirely from PostgreSQL

blocks.title: Three questions before adding one
items: Has the pain been measured: which query, how slow, how often?
Can the current database fix it with an index, a cache or an extension?
If the new one loses its data, can it be rebuilt from the main database?
Five databases in a small app to pad a CV: each one is another place where the system can break.
Writing to two databases one after the other (dual write): if one succeeds and the other fails, you have two truths.

items.label: Writing safely to two places: the outbox
The price of every new technology

check.q: If you add a separate search engine, where does the truth about orders live, and what is the search index?
check.a: The truth stays in PostgreSQL. The search index is a copy (derived data): if it breaks, delete it and rebuild it from the main database.

slides.title: The same order in six shapes
slides.tldr: One order looks different in each database family; the shape decides which questions are one line and which are impossible.

blocks.body: Take one order, number 1001: Nicole bought 2 of product P55 for $60. Each family writes it down in its own shape, and the shape decides which questions are easy and which are painful. Read the "easy" and "gives up" lines under each shape.

blocks.code:
RELATIONAL: rows in linked tables
  orders       id=1001  customer_id=7  total=6000
  order_items  order_id=1001  product_id=55  qty=2
  easy: sales per state (join + GROUP BY)
  gives up: easy write scaling over many servers
DOCUMENT: one JSON for the whole order
  orders/1001 = {"customer": "Nicole", "items": [{"sku": "P55", "qty": 2}], "total": 6000}
  easy: show the whole order in one read
  gives up: join with today's product prices
KEY-VALUE: one key, one opaque value
  order:1001 = <bytes>
  easy: GET order:1001
  gives up: "all orders of customer 7"
WIDE-COLUMN: rows grouped by partition key
  orders_by_customer  PARTITION KEY (customer_id)  SORTED BY created_at
    (7, 2025-01-05, 1001, 6000)
  easy: customer 7's latest orders
  gives up: "orders by state" (needs a second table, a copy)
GRAPH: nodes and edges
  (Nicole)-[:PLACED]->(Order 1001)-[:CONTAINS]->(Product P55)
  easy: "who bought what people like Nicole bought"
  gives up: a cheap sum of all totals
TIME-SERIES: a timestamp and a measurement
  cpu_load  time=10:00:01  server=web1  value=0.42
  easy: average of web1 over the last hour
  gives up: editing a row from last week

marks.tip: The customer and the items live in separate tables; the database joins them when you ask. That joining is what makes any later question possible.
Everything about the order sits in one place, so one read returns it all. But "today's price of P55" lives elsewhere, and you must fetch and combine it in your code.
The only way in is the key. If you did not plan a key for "orders of customer 7", the only option is scanning everything.

aside.body: Look at the shape first: every family is easy at the questions its shape was built for, and painful at the rest.

check.q: Your app must answer "all orders placed in Texas this month". Which of the six shapes above makes that a one-line question?
check.a: The relational one: one join and a GROUP BY. Key-value cannot search inside values at all, and wide-column would need a second copy of the data keyed by state.

slides.title: One fact, three places, three versions
slides.tldr: Write the same fact in several places and one day the copies drift apart; then nobody can say which one is right.

blocks.title: The store's house-account book
blocks.body: A store owner writes the customer's name and phone number beside every line of the house-account book, where the owner records who owes what. Mr Miller's number changes. The owner writes the new number on one line, and the other two lines keep the old one. At month end the owner goes to call and can't tell which number is real. Write the same fact again and again in your table and exactly this happens.

blocks.caption: The customer_order table, with name and phone copied into every row

rows.tip: The first order has Steven's name and his old number. Everything was correct at that point.
The spelling differs: someone typed it by hand in this row. Now one person has two names.
Steven changed his number, but only the new order picked it up. The two earlier rows still hold the old one.

blocks.body: Every place you write a fact is a place you must update it, and forgetting just one makes your data lie.

items.meaning: The fixed design of tables, columns and the relationships between them.
A fact stored in several rows is changed in one, and the others are left stale.

aside.title: Which number do I call?
aside.body: A courier company had copied the customer's address into every row of its orders table. A customer moved and placed a new order. The parcel for the old order still went to the old address, because the delivery app was reading that row.

check.q: If a customer's phone number is copied into every order row, what is the risk when the number changes?
check.a: Some rows will have the new number and some the old one. One person ends up with two different truths, and there is no way to know which is right.

slides.title: Normalization: one home for every fact
slides.tldr: Normalization means storing each fact once, in its own table; everything else holds only its ID (a foreign key).

blocks.title: A separate page per customer
blocks.body: This time the owner opens one page in the book for each customer, with the name and number written exactly once. An account line just says "page 12". When the number changes, the owner fixes it on that one page and everybody sees the new number. The page is a table row, the page number is the primary key, and the "page 12" on a account line is the foreign key.

blocks.caption: The phone number lives only in the customer table; the others point to it by ID

nodes.label: customer
nodes.tip: The name and phone number exist here once. To change them you change a single row.

nodes.label: customer_order
nodes.tip: The order holds no name or phone, only customer_id: the page number of the customer it belongs to.

nodes.label: order_item
nodes.tip: An order can contain many products, so each product gets its own row.

nodes.label: product
nodes.tip: The product's name and price are stored here exactly once.

edges.label: The order keeps only the customer_id
edges.tip: This customer_id is the foreign key. When the name or phone is needed, it is read from the customer table.

edges.label: Every item is part of one order
The item keeps only the product_id
One customer can have many orders
edges.tip: This is a one-to-many relationship: one customer, many orders.

blocks.title: The rule in three lines
items: One value per cell, never a comma-separated list (phone: '017.., 018..' is not allowed).
Each fact lives in the table of the thing that owns it: the name goes in customer, not in order.
Every column in a row must describe that row's subject and nothing else.

blocks.file: Changing Steven's number, before and after
blocks.code:
-- Before: the number sits in every order row
UPDATE customer_order SET customer_phone = '555-0102'
WHERE customer_name = 'Steven Miller';   -- misses the row typed 'Stephen Miller'

-- After: the number sits in one row, so one UPDATE is the whole job
UPDATE customer SET phone = '555-0102' WHERE id = 12;

marks.tip: Finding Steven's rows by name only works if every copy is spelled the same. Order 102 is not matched, so it keeps the old number.
The customer has one row, found by its id, so there is no copy to forget.

aside.body: The rule: write a fact once, and refer to it by ID from everywhere else.

items: The price: showing an order with the customer's name now needs a JOIN. With an index on customer_id that is fast. The next slides cover guards, and the last one the cases where a copy is the better choice.

items.meaning: The column that identifies a row uniquely.
A column that holds the primary key value of a row in another table.
The formal name for the three-line rule above.

check.q: What do you gain by storing customer_id in the order row instead of customer_name?
check.a: To change a name or phone you edit one row in the customer table. Every order reads the name from that single truth, so nothing can disagree.

slides.title: Constraints: the database as a guard
slides.tldr: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK stop bad data from entering inside the database itself, even when the code gets it wrong.

blocks.body: Form validation only guards the browser and the controller. But data also gets in through import scripts, console commands, old code and the endpoint everyone forgot about. So put a last guard in the database itself: a constraint. A bad row simply cannot get in, whichever way it tries.

marks.tip: UNIQUE: the same product cannot appear in two rows of the same order. To add it again you raise the quantity.
nullable: false means NOT NULL. Because of the FK, the order with this order_id must really exist in its table.
RESTRICT: a product that is in any order cannot be deleted. The order history never ends up orphaned.
CHECK: if the condition is false, the database rejects the row. Doctrine attributes have no CHECK, so add it in a migration with addSql().

blocks.caption: The four constraints: which mistake each one stops

rows.tip: Make anything NOT NULL if the row is meaningless without it.
Even if two people sign up at the same moment, the second is blocked. A "check first" in code cannot promise that.

cells: A customer_id that does not exist
rows.tip: Without an FK, the orders of a deleted customer are left dangling.
Simple business rules, such as a price that cannot be negative.

blocks.body: Code changes and there is more of it every year; data stays. The database is the last guard of the rules.

items: Show friendly errors with the validator (`UniqueEntity`), and also catch `UniqueConstraintViolationException` around `flush()`: when two requests race, only the database stops the second.
Adding a constraint to a big live table means cleaning bad rows first; see [[data/zero-downtime-migrations/alter-table-freeze|migrations without downtime]].

check.q: Is it enough to check that an email is unique in the Symfony validator, or do you need UNIQUE in the database too?
check.a: You need it in the database too. The validator "looks first, then writes", and two simultaneous requests can both pass. Only a UNIQUE constraint stops the second one.

slides.title: When copying is right, and when it is not
slides.tldr: Copy a snapshot of facts that change over time but must stay fixed in history (price, address); normalize the rest.

blocks.body: The opposite mistake exists too: normalizing everything and reading an order's price from the product's current price. If a product goes from $10 to $12, last month's invoice for 3 of them quietly changes from $30 to $36. So the price at the moment of the order must be copied into the order's own row. That is legitimate denormalization: a copy made on purpose, for a known reason.

blocks.file: Dangerous: reading the price through a join
blocks.code:
SELECT SUM(p.price_in_cents * oi.quantity) AS total
FROM order_item oi
JOIN product p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE oi.order_id = 130;

marks.tip: p.price_in_cents is the product's price today. If the price changes tomorrow, the total of the old order changes too.

blocks.file: Safe: the price at order time, in the row itself

marks.tip: Old rows get today's price once, the best value we have. From now on the order code copies `$product->getPriceInCents()` into every new order_item when it is created, and it never changes afterwards.
No join is needed and the result is always the same: 3 × $10 = $30, even after the price becomes $12. This is a snapshot.

blocks.caption: Which copies are fine and which are a danger

columns.title: Copying is fine
items: The price and address at the moment of the order (snapshot)
items_count on the order, changed in the same transaction as the order
A separate summary table for reports, built from the main data
columns.tip: Every such copy has a clear reason behind it: freezing history, or removing a query that has been measured as slow.

columns.title: Copying is a danger
items: customer_name on every order, which is supposed to match the customer's name
Copying early because "the join will be slow", without knowing
A copy exists, but nobody wrote down who updates it
columns.tip: Cases where the copy should follow the original when it changes, but nobody has arranged for that to happen.

use: A value that may change later but must stay as it was in old records (price, address, tax rate)
You measured that the join really is slow, and it is settled who updates the copy
avoid: Copying only because "we won't need a join later"
Facts that should always show the current value (a customer's current name)

items.label: If a join is slow, look at indexes first

check.q: Is copying each product's price into the order row for an invoice a normalization mistake?
check.a: No, it is a deliberate snapshot. A change to the product price must never alter an old invoice total, so the copy has a clear reason.

slides.title: Millions of rows, all read every time
slides.tldr: With no index, the database reads every row of the table for each query; 10 thousand rows go unnoticed, 2 million do not.

blocks.title: The library catalog
blocks.body: A library holds 2 million books. To find "Walden by Henry David Thoreau", you walk the shelves and check every book from the first to the last. Go to the catalog cards instead, sorted by author, and you get "shelf 14, third row" straight away. A database index is exactly that catalog: a sorted list where each entry says where the row is.

In Ryan's app the `customer_order` table has 2 million rows. The "My orders" page was fast a week ago and now takes about 0.4 seconds every time. The code hasn't changed at all; only the number of rows has grown. The fix is one line, shown below. The rest of this segment is about doing it well, and what it costs.

blocks.caption: Time to find customer_id = 42 in a table of 2 million rows

items.label: Without an index
items.tip: The database read all 2 million rows, then picked out 20. This is called a sequential scan.

items.label: With an index
items.tip: It followed the sorted list straight to customer 42's rows and never touched the other 1.9 million or so.

blocks.body: Without an index, every lookup reads the whole table. Add rows and the time grows at the same rate.

aside.title: The month before Black Friday
aside.body: An e-commerce site's "My orders" page ran in 50ms at the start of the year. In the Black Friday shopping month, orders piled up and it reached 3 seconds. The only cause was a missing index.

items.meaning: Reading every row of the table, from the first to the last.
A separate list sorted by a column's values, telling you where each row is.

check.q: Why is the same query fast on 10 thousand rows and slow on 2 million?
check.a: With no index, the database reads every row each time. So 200 times more rows means roughly 200 times more reading.

slides.title: What a B-tree index really is
slides.tldr: A B-tree is a sorted tree: from the root, three or four steps down reach any value, and because neighbors sit together, ranges and ORDER BY are cheap too.

blocks.title: The catalog drawers
blocks.body: A big catalog drawer is labeled "Q to Z". Inside it, a smaller slot says "Ta to Th", and in that slot are the individual cards. At every step most of the remaining cards drop out of the search. Because the cards are in order, lifting out everything from "Taylor" to "Thoreau" in one go is easy too.

blocks.caption: The journey of finding customer_id = 42 in a B-tree

nodes.label: query
nodes.tip: The value being looked for.

nodes.label: root page
nodes.tip: The top of the tree. It records which range of values goes down which branch.

nodes.label: branch page
nodes.tip: A middle level. It narrows the range further and points to the next level down.

nodes.label: leaf page
nodes.tip: The bottom level. It holds the sorted values and the location of each row. Leaves are linked to their neighbors, which makes reading a range easy.

nodes.label: table rows
nodes.tip: The leaf's location is used to read the actual rows.

edges.label: The search starts at the root page
42 falls in the 1 - 10K branch, so it goes down there
A narrower range still: it arrives at the 40 - 45 leaf
Following the leaf's locations, it fetches just 20 rows

blocks.title: Because it is sorted, three jobs are cheap
items: Lookup by value: even with 2 million rows, the tree is only 3 or 4 levels high.
Ranges: created_at BETWEEN ... The leaves sit side by side, so it is one continuous read.
ORDER BY: the data is already in order, so no separate sort is needed.

aside.body: B-tree = a sorted tree. You get lookup, ranges and ORDER BY, all three.

items: The default index in PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB) is a B-tree. You rarely need to say "B-tree" explicitly.
Searching from the middle of a value, such as LIKE '%abc', cannot use the sorted tree.

check.q: Why is a B-tree index useful for ORDER BY and range queries too?
check.a: Because the values in the leaves are stored in order. A range of values can be read in one run, and the result comes out already sorted, with no separate sort.

slides.title: Composite index: column order
slides.tldr: Column order in a composite index decides which queries it helps: equality columns first, range or sort columns after, and a condition must start from the left or the index is useless.

blocks.title: The phone book rule
blocks.body: A phone book is sorted by surname first, then by first name. Finding "Miller" and then "Kevin" inside that is easy. But if you only know "Kevin" you would have to leaf through the whole book. This is the leftmost prefix rule: an index works only for conditions that start from its leftmost column.

marks.tip: Name the index yourself, so you can recognize it in EXPLAIN and in migrations.
The equality column (customer_id) first, the sorting column (created_at) after. This order lets one index serve "my orders, newest first".

blocks.caption: Which queries the index (customer_id, created_at) helps

rows.tip: The search goes by the first column, so the index is fully used.
Within each customer_id, created_at is in order, so no separate sort is needed.
Equality, then a range. Both columns are used.

cells: No, the left column is skipped
rows.tip: Without the first column you cannot even begin. Like searching the phone book by first name only.
The same two columns in the opposite order help a different set of queries. The order is a decision, not a detail.

blocks.body: Column order: equality conditions first, then the range or ORDER BY column. And if a condition does not start from the left, the index is useless.

items: Two separate single-column indexes usually do not do the work of one well-chosen composite index.
Write the query first, then the index. Do not create one because "that column might get searched".

items.label: Cursor pagination needs exactly this index

check.q: With an index on (customer_id, created_at), why will a query with only WHERE created_at > ... not use it?
check.a: The index is sorted by customer_id first. created_at is sorted only inside each customer_id, so without the first column there is no way into it.

slides.title: Reading a query plan with EXPLAIN
slides.tldr: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) shows how the database really ran the query; Seq Scan turning into Index Scan means the index works, and a covering index even skips the table rows.

blocks.body: Creating an index does not mean the database uses it. To be sure, put `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` in front of the query. It really runs the query and shows the plan along with actual timings. First, glance for which "Scan" words appear.

blocks.code:
Limit  (actual time=410.8..412.5 rows=20 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=410.8..410.9 rows=20 loops=1)
        Sort Key: created_at DESC
        ->  Seq Scan on customer_order
              (actual time=0.02..408.9 rows=20 loops=1)
              Filter: (customer_id = 42)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 1999980
Execution Time: 412.7 ms

marks.tip: Seq Scan: reading the whole table. On a big table this is the red flag.
Rows Removed by Filter is nearly 2 million: rows read and thrown away. It touched 2 million rows to get 20.

blocks.file: After adding the index, then a covering index
blocks.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_order_customer_created
  ON customer_order (customer_id, created_at);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total_in_cents FROM customer_order
WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Index Scan Backward using idx_order_customer_created
-- Execution Time: 0.12 ms

-- Covering: keep the query's columns in the index itself
CREATE INDEX idx_order_customer_cov
  ON customer_order (customer_id, created_at)
  INCLUDE (total_in_cents);
-- Now the plan shows Index Only Scan: no table rows touched

marks.tip: Index Scan Backward: the newest-first sorted index is being read from the far end. There is no separate Sort step.
From 412ms to 0.12ms. This number is the real proof.
INCLUDE: this column is copied into the leaf. If the index holds all the query's columns, the real table need not be visited.

items.desc: Only the plan; it does not run the query
Really runs it and shows actual timings

items: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the query. For an INSERT or UPDATE, run it inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.
On a small table the database picks Seq Scan on purpose, because it is cheaper. Test with production-sized data.
A covering index (INCLUDE) makes the index bigger and every write costlier. Keep it for your one or two hottest queries.

check.q: What do you conclude when EXPLAIN shows "Seq Scan" and "Rows Removed by Filter: 1999980"?
check.a: The database read the whole table and threw away nearly every row. There is no index in the right order on the filter column, or the database is not using it.

slides.title: The price of indexes: writes get slower
slides.tldr: Every index speeds up reads but must also be updated on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE; keep only the useful ones, and use partial indexes to keep them small.

blocks.title: The catalog when a new book arrives
blocks.body: A new book arrives at the library. A card must go into the author catalog, another into the subject catalog, another into the publisher catalog. The more catalogs there are, the slower it is to shelve a book. A database is the same: every new row has to be inserted in the right place in every index.

blocks.caption: 2 indexes versus 10 indexes on one table

columns.title: 2 working indexes
items: Each INSERT: 1 table write + 2 index writes = 3 writes
Less disk space
Every index serves some query
columns.tip: Each index exists for some important query, and the extra cost on writes is small.

columns.title: 10 "might need" indexes
items: Each INSERT: 1 table write + 10 index writes = 11 writes
The indexes can grow bigger than the table
An unused index is just dead weight
columns.tip: Most of these indexes are never read, yet every write updates all of them.

marks.tip: Partial index: only pending orders go into the index. The tens of millions of completed orders do not weigh it down. In Doctrine you can pass where through options (PostgreSQL).

blocks.body: Every index makes reads faster and every write slower. Keep only the indexes that some query actually uses.

items.cmd: SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0;
items.desc: Indexes that have never been used

items: A partial index is used only when the query repeats its condition (WHERE status = 'pending'). Leave the condition out and the database cannot use it.
Before dropping an index, check that idx_scan stayed at zero over several weeks of full traffic, month-end reports included.
On tables that are written to very often (logs, events), keep indexes to the bare minimum.

check.q: Why do many indexes slow writes down, and how does a partial index help?
check.a: Every write must update every index too. A partial index holds only rows that match its condition, so it stays small and many writes never touch it.

slides.title: Same SQL, a different engine inside
slides.tldr: The storage engine inside a database decides which jobs are fast and which are slow, so one engine is not equally good for write-heavy and read-heavy work.

blocks.title: Two kinds of store ledger
blocks.body: In one store, every sale is written straight into the right page of the main ledger, which is kept in alphabetical order. It is easy to look things up, but each write means opening the book and finding the spot. In another store, every sale is first jotted down one after another on a pad at the counter, then sorted and copied into the main ledger in the evening. These two stores are a picture of the two kinds of engine.

blocks.caption: When the workload changes, so does the engine's advantage

columns.title: Read-heavy app
items: An online shop's products and order views
100 reads for every write
Finding any row quickly is what matters
columns.tip: Data is read a lot and written little. Here the sorted ledger (B-tree) is the most comfortable fit.

columns.title: Write-heavy app
items: Sensors, logs, chat, events: 1,000 sensors reporting every second is 1,000 writes a second
New data is only appended
Write speed is the real bottleneck
columns.tip: Thousands of new rows arrive every second and reads are comparatively rare. An accumulate-then-sort engine (LSM) suits this better.

blocks.body: The SQL is the same, but the engine inside decides which jobs are cheap and which are expensive.

aside.body: When choosing a database, "does it have SQL?" is not enough. You need to know how data lands on disk inside, because that sets the cost of reads and writes.

items.label: Choosing a database by the workload

check.q: Two databases both understand SQL, yet one is faster at writes and the other at reads. Why?
check.a: Their storage engines differ. One places data in its sorted spot as it arrives (fast reads); the other collects first and sorts later (fast writes).

slides.title: B-tree versus LSM-tree
slides.tldr: A B-tree finds the right spot at write time, so reads are good; an LSM-tree collects writes first and sorts later, so writes are good.

blocks.title: The main ledger versus the counter pad
blocks.body: A B-tree is the sorted main ledger: every new entry means finding the page and fitting it into the right line, so writes are slower, but any customer's account is found on one page. An LSM is the counter pad: write whatever comes, one after another, fast. The sorting has to happen later in the evening, and to look something up you may have to check both the pad and the older pages.

blocks.caption: The same job on two engines

columns.title: B-tree
items: Write: find the right page and put it there
Read: walk down the tree and land directly on it
Writes land in scattered places, so random writes on disk
A full page is split in two, which costs extra writes
columns.tip: The engine of PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB). Data lives in sorted pages, and a write modifies a page in place.

columns.title: LSM-tree
items: Write: collect in memory, only append on disk
Read: may have to check several files
Sequential writes on disk, which are fast
Compaction runs in the background
columns.tip: The engine of Cassandra and RocksDB. New writes are always appended at the end, then sorted in the background.

blocks.title: Three names for this trade-off
items: Write amplification: how many times the disk is really written for one write. A B-tree rewrites a whole page (8 to 16 KB) for a 100-byte change; an LSM rewrites data again at each compaction.
Read amplification: how many places must be checked to find one value.
Space amplification: how much more space is used than the real data needs.

aside.body: B-tree is a friend to reads, LSM is a friend to writes. But both have a price.

items: LSM reads can be made fast too (a Bloom filter tells you early "it's not in this file"), but it is not as simple as a B-tree.
The numbers matter less than the kind of work: choose by your own access pattern.

check.q: Why does an LSM-tree usually write fast in write-heavy workloads?
check.a: New writes gather in memory and are appended to the end of the disk, which is sequential. There is no need to hunt for scattered pages and modify them as a B-tree does.

slides.title: WAL, memtable, SSTable and compaction
slides.tldr: A write goes first to the WAL (safety), then to memory (speed), and to a disk file when memory fills; later compaction merges files and clears old and duplicate data.

blocks.title: The daybook and the counter pad
blocks.body: Before doing anything, the store owner writes "sold this much today" in the daybook. Even if the power goes out, the owner can rebuild everything from the daybook. That is the WAL. When the pad fills up, its contents are put away in a file, and every so often all the files are merged into one new sorted file that has no struck-out or outdated lines. That is compaction.

blocks.caption: The path a write takes in an LSM-tree

nodes.label: App
nodes.tip: Sends a new write.

nodes.label: WAL
nodes.tip: Write-ahead log: the write goes here first. If the server crashes, everything is rebuilt by reading this.

nodes.label: memtable
nodes.tip: A sorted list in memory. Both reads and writes are fast here.

nodes.label: SSTable file
nodes.tip: When the memtable fills, it goes to disk in sorted form. Once written, it never changes.

nodes.label: compaction
nodes.tip: Merges many small files into a big sorted one, clearing old values and deleted rows.

edges.label: It is written to the WAL first, so nothing is lost in a crash
The same write is placed in the in-memory memtable too
When the memtable fills, it goes to disk as a sorted SSTable file
Later, compaction merges many files into one clean file

blocks.body: Picture the memtable holding the last 10,000 writes, only in RAM, when the power goes. Without a WAL they are gone. With one, the server restarts, reads the log and puts all 10,000 back.
Write to the WAL first, then do the rest. After a crash, the database comes back by reading the WAL.

items.meaning: Writing any change to a sequential log before applying it in its real place.
Sorted String Table: a sorted disk file that is never changed once written.
Merging many files into a new one, leaving out old and deleted data.

aside.title: B-trees have a WAL too
aside.body: The WAL is not only for LSM. PostgreSQL writes every change to the WAL before the data page, and MySQL InnoDB does the same with its redo log. PostgreSQL replication follows this WAL; MySQL replicates through a separate binary log.

check.q: In an LSM-tree, writes sit in memory; why is no data lost when the server crashes?
check.a: Every write is first appended to the WAL on disk. After a crash, the database reads the WAL and rebuilds the memtable's data.

slides.title: Which database uses which engine, and when
slides.tldr: PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB) are B-tree based; Cassandra, ScyllaDB and RocksDB are LSM based. For ordinary business apps, B-tree is the default.

blocks.caption: The two families compared

rows.tip: LSM has more write capacity, because sequential writes to disk are cheap.

cells: Good, but may check several files
rows.tip: In a B-tree you just walk down the tree to find a value. In an LSM you may need to check the memtable and several levels of files.
In an LSM, compaction eats disk and CPU; under extreme load, write speed can suddenly drop.

cells: Old copies pile up, cleared by compaction
rows.tip: Both use more space than the data itself, for different reasons.
MongoDB's WiredTiger is B-tree by default, though it has an LSM option. Redis mostly lives in memory, a different kind.

blocks.title: Rules for deciding
items: Ordinary business apps (orders, users, payments; tens to hundreds of writes a second): B-tree, meaning PostgreSQL or MySQL.
Huge continuous writes with known queries (logs, sensors, chat; tens of thousands of writes a second and up): consider an LSM-based database.
If you are unsure, B-tree. Measure first, then change.

use: LSM: writes far outnumber reads, and data is mostly appended
B-tree: linked data, joins, transactions, any question
avoid: An LSM database in a small app just because it sounded "new and fast"

items.label: Choosing a database by the workload
Sharding, when one server cannot cope

check.q: What kind of engine is the usual choice for the main database of orders and payments?
check.a: A B-tree-based relational database (PostgreSQL or MySQL). Linked data, transactions and any query are easy there, and the write load usually fits on one server.

slides.title: Turning off durability because it feels slow
slides.tldr: Turning off fsync makes writes fast but a crash can corrupt the whole database; for data you can afford to lose, switch off synchronous_commit inside a single transaction instead.

blocks.body: When INSERTs feel slow, many people set `fsync = off`, because without forcing data to disk the numbers look great. But then a power cut can leave the database files themselves damaged, with half-written data. `synchronous_commit` is different: turning it off can lose only the last fraction of a second of commits (up to about 0.6 s by default), and the files are not corrupted.

blocks.code:
fsync = off                # dangerous: a crash can destroy the database
full_page_writes = off     # dangerous

marks.tip: It says "done" without making sure the data reached the disk. Never in production.
SET LOCAL applies only to the current transaction. The rest of the app keeps the safe default. Use it only for data like click logs, where losing some is harmless.
Writing many rows in one transaction is far cheaper than a separate commit for each row.

blocks.body: Never turn durability off for money data. If writes are slow, batch them first, then tune.

items: Never use synchronous_commit = off for payments, orders or balances: data can be lost even after you reported "success".
A separate commit per row is the biggest cause. Writing many rows in one transaction is the first remedy.

items.label: Durability is the D in ACID

check.q: What is the big difference between fsync = off and synchronous_commit = off?
check.a: Turning off fsync can corrupt the whole database in a crash. Turning off synchronous_commit leaves the files intact and can lose only the last fraction of a second of commits.

slides.title: Slow INSERTs: batch before you tune
slides.tldr: Every commit waits for one disk flush. 1,000 single-row commits wait 1,000 times; one transaction of 1,000 rows waits once, and risks nothing.

blocks.body: A commit doesn't return until its WAL record is flushed to disk, like a store clerk who won't hand over the receipt until the sale is written in the daybook. On a typical cloud disk one flush takes a few milliseconds; say 5 ms. Saving 1,000 click rows one by one means 1,000 flushes, about 5 seconds. Saving them in one transaction means 1 flush, about 5 ms, plus the inserts themselves.

blocks.caption: Time to store 1,000 rows when one flush takes 5 ms

items.label: 1,000 commits
items.tip: Autocommit: each INSERT is its own transaction, so each one waits for its own flush. 1,000 x 5 ms.

items.label: 1 transaction
items.tip: One flush (5 ms) plus the 1,000 inserts themselves. Roughly 80 times faster, and no durability given up.

marks.tip: Nothing wraps the loop, so PostgreSQL commits after every single row.
Chunks, not one giant transaction: a huge one holds locks for long, and one bad row rolls back all of it.

items: Doctrine's `$em->flush()` already runs all pending changes in one transaction. Call it once per batch, not once per entity.

use: Many rows arrive together: imports, event batches, a queue consumer.
avoid: Rows arriving one at a time from separate web requests: there is nothing to batch. Collect them in a queue first, or use SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off for loss-tolerant data.

check.q: Why are 1,000 single-row commits far slower than one transaction of 1,000 rows?
check.a: Each commit waits for its own disk flush. 1,000 commits wait 1,000 times (about 5 seconds at 5 ms each); one transaction waits once.

slides.title: IDs like take-a-number tickets: simple, but limited
slides.tldr: Auto-increment IDs are simple and small, but they can be guessed, they leak the size of your business, and they collide when several databases or servers generate them.

blocks.title: Take-a-number tickets at a deli
blocks.body: At a deli counter, tickets go 1, 2, 3: short, in order, one after another. But if the deli has two branches, both hand out a "ticket 1", and a ticket number alone no longer identifies anyone. And anyone who sees ticket 43 knows at least 43 customers have come by and can guess that number 44 exists. A database's auto-increment ID has exactly these three problems.

blocks.caption: The strengths of auto-increment, and its limits

columns.title: What is good
items: Small: a bigint is only 8 bytes
Always appended at the end of the index, so fast
The database makes it, no code needed
columns.tip: This is why it is the default in most apps, and used properly it is a good choice.

columns.title: What is a problem
items: Guessable: /invoices/1042 -> /invoices/1043
Leaks business size: 1042 today and 1100 tomorrow means 58 orders
IDs collide across two databases
You must insert first to learn the ID
columns.tip: These problems go unnoticed in a small app. They appear when the app grows or when outsiders can see the IDs.

blocks.body: An ID is an identity, not a secret. If IDs can be guessed, put your security somewhere else.

aside.title: The competitor's scraper
aside.body: An e-commerce site used sequential numbers for order IDs. A competitor placed an order at the same time each day, noted the ID, and subtracted to learn how many orders the site got per day.

items.meaning: A counter inside the database that hands out the next number each time: 1, 2, 3...
Seeing someone else's data by changing an ID, because ownership is never checked.

check.q: How do sequential IDs leak business information?
check.a: Subtract the IDs from two different days and you know how many rows, such as orders or users, were created in between.

slides.title: Five kinds of ID side by side
slides.tldr: Sequence, UUIDv4, UUIDv7, ULID and Snowflake differ on four questions: size, sortable by time, guessability, and whether they need coordination.

blocks.title: Five ticket schemes
blocks.body: A sequential number is the plain ticket number. UUIDv4 is a random card number drawn in a lottery: nobody can guess it, but it is not in any order. UUIDv7 and ULID are numbers that start with a date, like "2026-05-12-734": the date first makes them sortable, and the random tail makes them hard to guess. A Snowflake has the date, then which branch issued it and the branch's own running number.

blocks.caption: The five IDs at a glance

rows.tip: One database does the counting. Generate from several places and the IDs collide.
122 bits of pure randomness. It can be made anywhere, but it scatters across a B-tree index.
48 bits of time first, then random. It keeps every UUID benefit and sorts by time, which makes it the best default for a new project today.
Almost the same idea as UUIDv7, but written as a shorter alphanumeric string that also sorts. v7 is usually simpler because tools support UUIDs better.
Time + machine id + counter, 64 bits in total, fits in a bigint. Every server must be given a distinct machine id, and that is the coordination.

blocks.title: Which one, when
items: One database, IDs never shown outside: a sequence is enough.
IDs shown outside, or generated in several places: UUIDv7.
Huge scale and you need a small bigint ID: a Snowflake-style ID (if you can manage the machine ids).

aside.body: In a new project, when in doubt: a sequence or UUIDv7 internally, UUIDv7 externally.

items: The price of a 16-byte ID: every secondary index in MySQL InnoDB carries a copy of the primary key. On 100 million rows, 8 extra bytes is about 0.8 GB more per index.

items.label: Machine ids and which server handles what

check.q: What is the main difference between UUIDv4 and UUIDv7?
check.a: v4 is entirely random, so it is not ordered. v7 starts with the time, so a new ID comes after older ones, while its random tail keeps it hard to guess.

slides.title: Why random IDs tire out the index
slides.tldr: A primary key lives in a B-tree. A random UUIDv4 writes to any leaf of the tree each time (pages split, caches miss); a time-sorted ID is appended to the last leaf.

blocks.title: A guest book sorted by ticket number
blocks.body: Names are written into a guest book in ticket-number order. If each new customer's ticket number is always bigger than the last, you just write on the last page, and only one page is ever open. But if the numbers arrive at random, every time you must open the book somewhere in the middle and squeeze an entry in, and sometimes tear a page in two to make room.

blocks.caption: Where a new row lands in the primary key index

columns.title: UUIDv4 (random)
items: Inserts scatter over every page
A full page splits in two (page split)
The right page may not be in the cache
The index becomes hollow and large
columns.tip: Each insert falls on any page of the tree. If the pages do not all fit in memory, they must be read from disk.

columns.title: UUIDv7 / sequence
items: Inserts always go to the last page
Pages fill completely and split rarely
The last page stays hot in the cache
The index is dense and small
columns.tip: A new ID is always bigger than the earlier ones, so it is appended to one page at the right edge of the index. That page stays in memory.

blocks.caption: The 64 bits of a Snowflake: three parts

steps.title: 1. Time (41 bits)
steps.body: In milliseconds from a fixed start date. Lasts about 69 years.
steps.tip: Time comes first, which is why the ID sorts in time order.

steps.title: 2. Machine id (10 bits)
steps.body: Which server or worker made it. 1024 distinct ones.
steps.tip: Every running server needs its own id. Handing these out is the coordination work.

steps.title: 3. Counter (12 bits)
steps.body: Up to 4096 on the same machine in the same millisecond.
steps.tip: If many IDs are needed in one ms, the counter climbs. When it runs out, it must wait for the next ms.

blocks.body: The order of the primary key decides the health of the index. On a big table, choose time-sorted IDs, not random ones.

items: In MySQL InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index, meaning the whole table's data is stored in that order. So a random PK hurts even more there.
On a small table (a few hundred thousand rows that all fit in memory) you will barely notice the difference. The damage shows on big tables.

check.q: Why does a UUIDv4 primary key slow inserts on a big table while UUIDv7 does not?
check.a: v4 is random, so each insert lands on any leaf of the tree and pages split. v7 is sorted by time, so it is always appended to the last leaf.

slides.title: Using UUIDv7 with Symfony Uid
slides.tldr: With the Symfony Uid component, create `Uuid::v7()` in the constructor, give Doctrine a `UuidType`, and put `Requirement::UUID_V7` on the route; the ID is known before flush.

blocks.body: `composer require symfony/uid` brings in the Uid component. If you create the UUID in the constructor, the ID is known before it ever reaches the database, so you can use the order's ID straight away to arrange events or emails. In Doctrine the column type is `UuidType::NAME`, which stores it as a native `uuid` on PostgreSQL and as `BINARY(16)` on MySQL, both smaller than 36 characters of text.

marks.tip: There is no GeneratedValue, because we make the ID ourselves. Doctrine just stores it.
v7: sorted by time. Because the ID exists before the database insert, related objects can be given it immediately.
An id of the wrong kind gets a 404 before it ever reaches the controller.
Even when the ID is hard to understand, you still need an authorization check: use a voter to verify ownership.

blocks.title: A few small rules
items: For ULIDs, use the `Ulid` class and `UlidType::NAME` in the same way.
Show `toRfc4122()` (36 characters) outside; keep a native uuid or binary in the database.
A two-ID design also works, a bigint inside and a UUID outside, but handling two IDs adds hassle.

items.desc: The Uid component and the Doctrine type

items: Do not keep a UUID in a text column (varchar(36)). It takes more than double the space, and the index grows.

check.q: What is one benefit of putting Uuid::v7() in the entity's constructor?
check.a: The ID is known before the database insert. So you can hand it to an event, a log or another object without flushing first.

slides.title: A hard-to-guess ID is not security
slides.tldr: Even when IDs are hard to guess, you cannot skip authorization; and a UUIDv7 reveals when it was created, so think about that if the time must stay secret.

blocks.body: Many people think "if I use a UUID, nobody can see someone else's invoice anymore." But once an ID leaks through a link, a log or the browser history, anyone can use it. The real protection is to check on every request: "is this user the owner of this record?"

marks.tip: There is no ownership check. Change /invoices/1042 to 1043 and you see someone else's invoice: IDOR.
The voter runs on every request. This, not the UUID, is the main protection.
It checks only one thing: whether the invoice's owner is the current user.

blocks.body: Hiding an ID is not security. Check ownership on every request; a UUID is just an extra layer.

items: With UUIDv7, ULID or Snowflake, the creation time can be read from the ID. If that must stay secret (such as an account's sign-up date), use a separate random public token.
In a Snowflake, giving two servers the same machine id makes IDs collide, and a clock that jumps backwards can break IDs.

check.q: Even with UUIDs, why must you still check ownership before showing an invoice?
check.a: Because a UUID can leak through a link or a log. Being hard to guess is not security; protection comes from an authorization check on every request.

slides.title: The danger of a single copy
slides.tldr: When the only database server dies, everything stops, and one machine carries all the read load. Replication keeps several copies: one leader takes the writes and the followers receive copies.

blocks.title: The head office ledger and the branch copies
blocks.body: A bank keeps all its accounts only in the head office ledger. If the office burns down, everything is gone, and when everyone comes to check their balance the queue is long. So the head office also sends every new entry to the branches. New writes happen only at the head office (the leader); the other branches (the followers) keep copies and take over the viewing work.

blocks.caption: One leader, two followers: writes in one place, reads spread out

nodes.label: Symfony app
nodes.tip: Both write and read requests come from here.

nodes.label: leader
nodes.tip: The only node that accepts writes. It records every change in its WAL (write-ahead log, a diary of all changes) and sends it to the followers.

nodes.label: follower 1
nodes.tip: A copy of the leader. It serves read requests but takes no writes.

nodes.label: follower 2
nodes.tip: Another copy. If the leader dies, this one can also become the new leader.

edges.label: All writes go to the one leader
The leader sends every change to follower 1
The same change goes to follower 2 too
The read load is spread across the followers

blocks.title: What replication gives you
items: Survival: if the leader dies, a follower can be made the new leader.
Read capacity: more followers means more read requests handled.
Backups and reports: heavy queries run on a follower, which spares the leader.

aside.body: Replication does not increase write capacity: writes still go to a single leader. When the write load grows, you need sharding. A follower is also not a backup: a wrong `DELETE` on the leader is copied to every follower within moments.

items.label: Is a replica a substitute for a backup?

check.q: In replication, who handles writes and who handles reads?
check.a: Only the leader handles writes. Reads can be shared between the leader and the followers, since the followers hold copies of the leader's data.

slides.title: Sync versus async replication
slides.tldr: With async, the leader says "done" without waiting for followers: fast, but a crash can lose the latest writes. With sync, it waits: safer, but slower.

blocks.title: Sent by post, or confirmed by phone
blocks.body: If the head office posts a new entry to the branch, it finishes its own work right away, and the branch will get the letter tomorrow. That is async. If it phones to ask "did you receive it?" and only then tells the customer "it's done", that is sync. The post is fast, but if the head office burns down, the letters on their way are lost. The phone is safe, but if the branch line is busy, the customer stands waiting.

blocks.caption: The price of each approach

columns.title: Async (default)
items: The leader commits as soon as it has written to its own disk
Writes are fast and a slow follower does not hold them up
If the leader crashes, the commits of the last moments (a fraction of a second to a few seconds) may be lost
columns.tip: Most apps use this one. Write speed is the leader's own speed.

columns.title: Sync
items: The leader waits for at least one follower to confirm
Every write gains one network round trip: about 1 ms in the same data center, 50 ms or more to another region
If all the sync followers die, writes may stop too
columns.tip: Worth considering for data like money. Safer, but every write is slower.

blocks.code:
# a commit succeeds only after at least 1 follower confirms
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (replica1, replica2)'
synchronous_commit = on

marks.tip: ANY 1 (...): it is enough for any one follower to confirm. Writes do not stop even if one dies. This is called quorum-style sync.

blocks.body: Async means the risk of losing the last writes if the leader dies. Sync means a delay on every write. You have to pick one.

use: Async: most apps, where losing the last few seconds of writes in a crash is acceptable
Sync (ANY 1): money and orders, where data must not be lost after you say "success"
avoid: Keeping just one sync follower: if it dies, writes get stuck

items.label: The trade-off between speed and correctness

check.q: What risk does async replication carry when the leader crashes?
check.a: The last few commits may be lost, because the leader said "done" without waiting for the followers to confirm, and those commits never reached a follower.

slides.title: Lag: you can't see your own write
slides.tldr: An async follower runs a little behind (replication lag). Read from a follower right after a write and the user doesn't see their own new data; this problem is called read-your-own-writes.

blocks.body: Ryan writes a comment and presses "Send". The write goes to the leader, but when the page refreshes it reads from a follower that has not yet heard the news. Ryan sees that his comment is missing. He sends it again, and now there are two comments. The database is fine; the mistake lies in where the read came from.
