actors.tip: Writes a comment and refreshes the page at once.

actors.label: leader
actors.tip: The write goes here; the new comment is here.

actors.label: follower
actors.tip: About 2 seconds behind. It has not received the new comment yet.

messages.tip: It takes time for changes to travel from the leader to this follower. That is replication lag.

messages.label: List without #91
messages.tip: Ryan thinks his comment was lost.

blocks.body: Show people their own writes. Do the reads that matter right after a write from the leader.

aside.title: The double post
aside.body: On one social app, the feed after a post was served from a follower. Many people did not see their post and posted again, so the same text appeared two or three times.

items.meaning: The time a change on the leader takes to reach a follower.
The guarantee that you always see your own writes in later reads.

check.q: The write succeeded, yet reading straight after shows no new data. Did the database make a mistake?
check.a: No. The read went to a follower that was still behind (replication lag). The fix is to read from the leader for a short while after a write.

slides.title: A primary/replica setup in Doctrine
slides.tldr: With replicas in doctrine.yaml, DoctrineBundle sends reads to a replica and writes to the primary; after a write, every read in that request goes to the primary on its own, and a sticky listener handles the rest.

blocks.code:
doctrine:
  dbal:
    url: '%env(resolve:DATABASE_URL)%'        # primary
    replicas:
      replica1:
        url: '%env(resolve:DATABASE_REPLICA1_URL)%'
      replica2:
        url: '%env(resolve:DATABASE_REPLICA2_URL)%'

marks.tip: The main url is the primary: all writes, transactions and migrations go here.
With replicas present, DoctrineBundle automatically uses PrimaryReadReplicaConnection. One replica is picked at random for each request.

blocks.body: The rule is this: if nothing has been written yet, `executeQuery()` (find, SELECT) goes to a replica. But once a `flush()` or a transaction begins, every read and write for the rest of that request goes to the primary. So within one request you do see your own writes. The problem is only in the next request.

marks.tip: For about 5 seconds after a write, this user reads from the primary, giving the replica time to get past its lag.

blocks.body: After a write, add just one line to the controller: `$request->getSession()->set('primary_until', time() + 5);`. Then that user's reads for the next 5 seconds come from the primary, and by then the replica has usually caught up.

items: Not every read belongs on a replica: money figures, the first page after login and "my" data are safer on the primary.
The 5 seconds is a guess that must beat your real lag. Measure the lag; if it spikes above 5 seconds, widen the window. It costs you some read offloading for those users.

Once a request writes or opens a transaction, the `replicas` wrapper (DBAL's PrimaryReadReplicaConnection) keeps that request on the primary, so a read after your own write is safe within one request.
For something more elaborate, note the leader's WAL position (LSN) at write time and check whether the follower has reached it, though that takes extra work.

check.q: In Doctrine, why can you see your own write if you call find() later in the same request?
check.a: Once a flush or a transaction begins, PrimaryReadReplicaConnection switches to the primary, and every other query in that request runs on the primary too.

slides.title: Failover and split brain
slides.tldr: When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted to leader (failover); but if the old leader comes back alive and both take writes, you get split brain and the data divides in two.

blocks.title: Two head offices
blocks.body: When contact with the head office is cut, one branch thinks "I am the head office now." Then the old head office comes back, also convinced that it is in charge. Both take entries, and the two ledgers hold different accounts. That is split brain: two leaders, and neither ledger holds the whole truth.

blocks.caption: The steps of a safe failover

steps.title: 1. Is the leader dead?
steps.body: Agree on it through several checks, not one moment of network trouble.
steps.tip: A failover on a false signal creates a situation where the old leader is actually alive.

steps.title: 2. Stop the old one
steps.body: Shut down the old leader, or block its writes (fencing).
steps.tip: This is the step that prevents split brain. The old leader must never be able to take writes again.

steps.title: 3. Promote the furthest ahead
steps.body: Make the follower closest to the leader the new leader.
steps.tip: Promoting the follower that is least behind loses the fewest writes.

steps.title: 4. Tell the app
steps.body: The app sends writes to the new leader; the old one returns as a follower.
steps.tip: When the old leader returns, its extra writes must be discarded and it copies afresh from the new leader.

blocks.body: A failover that is not automatic cannot be relied on, and an automatic failover without fencing is dangerous.

items: Don't write your own hand-made failover script; use Patroni or the proven machinery of a managed database (RDS, Cloud SQL).
With async, a failover can lose the last few writes. You must know whether your business can live with that.
Rehearse failover regularly. A failover that was never tested will not work in an emergency.

items.label: Agreeing on who the leader is

check.q: What is split brain, and which failover step must exist to prevent it?
check.a: Split brain is two nodes both believing they are the leader and taking writes. To prevent it, the old leader must be fenced off from writing.

slides.title: Sharding is the last resort, not the first
slides.tldr: Sharding splits data across several servers. It adds huge complexity, so exhaust indexes, caching, a bigger server, replicas and partitioning first.

blocks.title: A delivery company's regional warehouses
blocks.body: A courier company keeps every parcel in one warehouse in Dallas. The warehouse fills up, and someone suggests opening one warehouse per region. That buys space, but now finding a Seattle parcel from Dallas takes a phone call, totaling stock across two regions is hard, and opening yet another warehouse means moving parcels around. They should have asked first whether the one warehouse could be organized better.

blocks.caption: The rungs to climb before sharding

steps.title: 1. Fix queries and indexes
steps.body: Measure slow queries, add indexes, remove N+1 (one query per row in a loop).
steps.tip: Most "the database can't cope" problems end right here. It is the cheapest step.

steps.title: 2. Add a cache
steps.body: Answer repeated reads before they reach the database.
steps.tip: A large share of the read load moves into the cache.

steps.title: 3. Get a bigger server
steps.body: More RAM, faster disks (vertical scaling).
steps.tip: Today's big servers handle a lot of data. You buy time without touching code.

steps.title: 4. Add read replicas
steps.body: Copy the data to follower servers and send reads there. The leader takes the writes.
steps.tip: This helps with read load. It does nothing for write load: every write still goes to the one leader.

steps.title: 5. Partition and archive
steps.body: Split big tables on one server, move old data out.
steps.tip: The table is cut into smaller pieces inside one database. The app doesn't change.

steps.title: 6. Then shard
steps.body: Only when one server's write limit is truly exceeded.
steps.tip: Roughly when one tuned server can't keep up with its writes, often thousands a second. From here on the app has to know which server holds the data. Complexity jumps.

blocks.body: Sharding is the last resort. Never shard before every simpler step is exhausted.

use: Writes (not reads) outgrow one big server even after steps 1 to 5.
The data no longer fits on one server's disk, even after archiving.
avoid: Because big companies do it. Their volume is not yours.
When reads are the bottleneck. Replicas and a cache fix that for far less.

items.meaning: Splitting one table into smaller pieces, usually on the same database server.
Putting those pieces on separate servers, so each server handles one slice of the data.

check.q: Your database write load keeps growing. Which steps do you try before sharding?
check.a: Fix slow queries and indexes, trim needless writes, buy a bigger server, archive or partition old data. A cache and replicas only relieve reads. If writes still outgrow one server, shard.

slides.title: The shard key and the router
slides.tldr: Every row has a shard key. A router computes which shard the row lives on, and the app talks straight to that shard.

blocks.title: The region code picks the warehouse
blocks.body: Every parcel carries a region code: 01 Dallas, 02 Chicago, 03 Seattle. The desk reads the code and says which warehouse the parcel goes to, and the same desk sends you to the same warehouse when you come looking for it. The code is the shard key, the desk is the router, and each warehouse is a shard. Pick the codes badly and one warehouse overflows.

blocks.caption: Picking one of 3 shards by customer_id

nodes.label: Symfony app
nodes.tip: The request carries a customer_id, and that is the shard key.

nodes.label: ShardRouter
nodes.tip: Computes the shard from the key. It can live inside the app or run as a separate proxy.

nodes.label: shard 0
nodes.tip: One third of the data, on its own database server.

nodes.label: shard 1
nodes.tip: Another third.

nodes.label: shard 2
nodes.tip: The rest. All of customer 42's orders live here.

edges.label: The app says: I need customer 42's orders
The router computes that 42 belongs on shard 2
Only shard 2 answers; the other two are never touched

blocks.title: Three ways to split
items: Range: by key ranges (1 to 1,000,000 goes to shard 0).
Hash: hash(key) % N, which spreads rows evenly.
Lookup: a separate table records which key lives on which shard.

aside.body: Shard key = the region code on the parcel. Get the code wrong and one warehouse is stuffed while the rest sit empty.

items: A query that includes the shard key goes to one shard. Without the key it has to visit every shard.

check.q: How does the app know which shard holds customer 42's orders?
check.a: The router computes it from the shard key (customer_id), for example hash(key) % number of shards. The same key always maps to the same shard, so reads go there too.

slides.title: The wrong key: one shard takes all the load
slides.tldr: A good shard key spreads load evenly, appears in most queries and never changes. A bad one (country, date) piles everything on one hot shard.

blocks.body: An e-commerce app has 4 shards, and the team chose the customer's country as the shard key. But 72% of customers are in the US, so one shard burns while three sleep. They bought four servers and only one is doing any work. Hash `customer_id` instead and each shard gets about a quarter of the customers, so each carries about 25%.

blocks.caption: Shard key = country: share of the load on each shard

items.label: shard 0 (US)
items.tip: The hot shard: nearly every read and write lands here. If it slows down, the whole app slows down.

items.label: shard 1 (CA)
items.tip: Customers from Canada. Idle most of the time.

items.label: shard 2 (UK)
items.tip: Barely working.

items.label: shard 3 (other)
items.tip: Almost unused.

blocks.title: Four traits of a good shard key
items: Many distinct values (high cardinality): customer_id is good, country is bad.
Load spreads evenly: no single value is hugely popular.
It appears in most queries, so one shard can finish the job.
Once set, it never changes.

blocks.caption: Strengths and risks of the three strategies

cells: All new data hits the latest shard: hot shard
rows.tip: With a date key, every write today lands on one shard while the older ones become read-only.

cells: Range queries hit every shard; changing N moves most data
rows.tip: The most common choice. But changing N directly moves most of the rows, which is why you need virtual buckets (next slides).

cells: Any key can move to any shard
The lookup table becomes a new bottleneck and single point of failure
rows.tip: Flexible, but every request consults it first, so you have to cache and replicate it.

items: The celebrity problem: even with customer_id as the key, one huge customer (or tenant) can fill a shard alone. Give big tenants their own shard through a lookup table.
Changing the shard key later means moving all the data. Think through the access patterns up front.

check.q: One shard carries 72% of the load. What could replace country as the shard key?
check.a: A hash of customer_id. It has many distinct values, so load spreads evenly, and since most queries include customer_id, one shard can do the whole job.

slides.title: In code: partitions and a shard router
slides.tldr: Start with PostgreSQL declarative partitions on one server. For real sharding, give Doctrine one connection per shard and a router built on virtual buckets.

marks.tip: The partition key (created_at) must be part of the primary key. Price: id alone is no longer guaranteed unique, only the pair (id, created_at).
Split by month: you can DETACH an old month and archive it, and queries only touch the partitions they need.
1024 virtual buckets to avoid a painful reshard: the key maps to a bucket first, and the bucket maps to a shard.
To move data you change only the bucket-to-shard map, never the bucket calculation, so the hashing stays put.

blocks.body: In `config/packages/doctrine.yaml`, name one connection per shard under `doctrine.dbal.connections` (`shard_0`, `shard_1`) and read each `url` from its own env variable. Then `$registry->getConnection('shard_0')` returns the DBAL connection for that shard. `$bucketToShard` is a 1024-entry map; the next slide shows where it lives and how to change it.

items: You would need a separate ORM EntityManager per shard. To keep things simple, use the DBAL Connection on shards.
Migrations must run on every shard separately. If you don't automate that, the shards drift into different schemas.
Pick the bucket count once: 1024 buckets means at most 1024 shards, and changing it later re-hashes everything.

items.label: Moving less data when N changes

check.q: What do 1024 virtual buckets buy you compared with plain hash % N?
check.a: Changing the number of shards doesn't change the hash calculation. You only edit the bucket-to-shard map and move some buckets to another shard, so not all the data moves.

slides.title: Adding a shard: move 20%, not 80%
slides.tldr: Going from 4 to 5 shards with hash % N moves 80% of the rows. With 1024 buckets you reassign about 205 buckets (20%), one at a time, while the app runs.

blocks.body: A shop has 100 million orders on 4 shards and adds a fifth. With `hash % N`, the `% 4` becomes `% 5`, and a row stays put only when both remainders agree: 1 row in 5. So 80 million rows travel. With buckets the hash never changes: the map starts with 256 buckets per shard, and the new shard takes about 51 from each old one. That is 205 buckets, 20 million rows, the least that has to move.

blocks.caption: Rows that move when a 5th shard joins 100 million rows

items.label: hash % N
items.tip: % 4 becomes % 5, so 4 of every 5 rows get a new home. Nearly a full copy of the database.

items.label: 1024 buckets
items.tip: Only the buckets handed to shard_4 move, about 205 of 1024. The new shard gets its fair fifth and nothing more.

blocks.file: The bucket map, kept in a small directory database

marks.tip: Buckets 0 to 255 start on shard_0, 256 to 511 on shard_1, and so on. The crc32 calculation in the router never changes.
The flip. From now on the router sends bucket 4 to shard_4. App servers must reload the map (load it at boot and refresh it every few seconds).

blocks.caption: Moving one bucket without losing a write

steps.title: 1. Dual write
steps.body: New writes for the bucket go to both shards. Reads stay on shard_0.
steps.tip: Switch this on first. Anything written while you copy then lands on shard_4 as well and is not lost.

steps.title: 2. Copy
steps.body: Copy the bucket's existing rows to shard_4, skipping rows already there.
steps.tip: Users keep working. shard_0 still serves every read.

steps.title: 3. Verify
steps.body: Compare row counts and checksums on both sides.
steps.tip: Trust nothing. A silent gap here becomes lost data after step 4.

steps.title: 4. Flip
steps.body: UPDATE the map. The router now reads shard_4.
steps.tip: One row changes, so the switch is instant and easy to undo by flipping it back.

steps.title: 5. Clean up
steps.body: After a safety wait, delete the bucket from shard_0.
steps.tip: Keep the old copy for a few days. It is your undo button.

items: Store the bucket number in each row (a `bucket` column, indexed). SQL can't compute crc32 for you, so this is how you select exactly one bucket's rows.
Move one bucket, check the dashboards, then the next. A slow trickle beats a weekend of copying.

use: You expect to add shards over the years, and rows must move in small, safe pieces.
avoid: The data fits on one server. A partitioned table is far simpler.
You only ever need a fixed number of shards and never grow. Plain hash % N is enough.

check.q: Going from 4 to 5 shards, why does hash % N move 80% of the rows but buckets only about 20%?
check.a: With hash % N the remainder changes for 4 rows in 5, so they all move. With buckets the hash is fixed and you only reassign about 205 of 1024 buckets to the new shard, which is the least that must move.

slides.title: Cross-shard queries and resharding
slides.tldr: A query without the shard key fans out to every shard (scatter-gather) and is slow. Joins and transactions across shards are hard, and resharding is painful, so plan ahead.

nodes.tip: And here. The slowest shard sets the time for the whole query.

blocks.title: What gets hard once you shard
items: Joins across shards: the database no longer does them, so the app must.
Transactions across shards: instead of ACID you need sagas or another approach.
Unique constraints across shards (such as email) stop working beyond one shard.
Reports and aggregates: collect data from every shard into a separate database first.

blocks.body: Split the data so that most queries finish on exactly one shard.

aside.title: Resharding took weeks
aside.body: A company filled its 4 shards and added a fifth. Switching from hash % 4 to % 5 moved 4 of every 5 rows. It took weeks of copying and verifying. Now they use virtual buckets from day one.

items: When resharding, write to both old and new places (dual write), verify, then switch over, as the previous slide shows. It is big work, so plan it.
If you need a very large database, consider a managed or distributed SQL system (CockroachDB, Vitess) that handles sharding for you.

check.q: Why is a query without the shard key so slow, and how do you avoid it?
check.a: Nobody knows which shard holds the data, so the query goes to all of them and the results are merged. Avoid it by choosing the key from your access patterns and adding a separate index or lookup table for other kinds of search.

slides.title: Refresh the page, travel back in time
slides.tldr: With several copies of the data, not everyone sees the same thing at the same moment. The rules for who sees what, and when, are called a consistency model.

blocks.title: The campus notice boards
blocks.body: A campus has three buildings and a notice board in each. When the dean writes a new notice, an assistant pins it up board by board. A student who sees the new notice on the first board may walk to the second building and not find it there, because the assistant hasn't arrived yet. The more copies you have, the more chances for a mismatch like this.

blocks.caption: Ryan refreshes twice, and the count goes down

actors.label: Ryan
actors.tip: Opens the same page twice in a row.

actors.label: replica A
actors.tip: Has already received the new comment.

actors.label: replica B
actors.tip: Still behind; it hasn't got the new comment yet.

messages.label: Refresh: show them again
messages.tip: This time the load balancer sent him to the other replica.

messages.label: 2 comments
messages.tip: Ryan just saw 3 and now sees 2. Time went backwards.

blocks.body: The more copies you have, the more it matters to decide who sees what, and when.

aside.title: The like count that came back
aside.body: In one app a post's like count went from 12 to 10 and back to 12 as you refreshed. Users thought the app was broken. In fact each request was landing on a different replica.

check.q: Two refreshes show the comment count drop from 3 to 2. Was data deleted?
check.a: No. The two requests hit different replicas: one had the new data and the other didn't yet. That is a consistency problem, not data loss.

slides.title: From strong to eventual: a ladder of rules
slides.tldr: Strong consistency always shows the latest data but is slower and less available. Eventual is the fastest but may show stale data for a while. A few handy rules sit in between.

blocks.title: Three rules for pinning notices
blocks.body: The strict rule: nobody reads anything until the notice is on every board. Everyone sees the same notice, but the wait is long, and if one building's assistant doesn't show up, everything stalls. The loose rule: read what is on your board and let the others catch up. That is fast, but the boards disagree for a while. The rules in between rule out specific kinds of disagreement.

blocks.caption: From strict to loose: safe but heavy at the top, fast but mismatch-prone at the bottom

layers.label: Strong (linearizable)
layers.tip: It behaves as if there were only one copy. Once a write finishes, every reader gets the new value. More delay, less availability.

layers.label: Causal
layers.tip: Nobody sees an answer before the question. Events that depend on each other keep their order.

layers.label: Read-your-writes
layers.tip: The person who wrote something sees it on their next read, even if others see it a bit later.

layers.label: Monotonic reads
layers.tip: Once you have seen newer data, a later read never shows older data.

layers.label: Eventual
layers.tip: For a while readers may see different things, but if no new writes arrive, all copies end up equal. The fastest option.

blocks.body: Strong buys you convenience and costs you latency and failure risk. Ask for it only where you really need it.

aside.body: Stricter means slower. For each piece of data, pick the loosest rule that doesn't confuse the user.

check.q: What does "eventual" mean in eventual consistency?
check.a: If writes stop, all copies will reach the same value after a while. In the meantime, copies may show different values.

slides.title: Seeing your own writes, and time moving forward
slides.tldr: Read-your-writes and monotonic reads are cheap to get: after a write, read from the primary when needed, and always send each user to the same replica.

blocks.caption: Two session guarantees: the problem and the fix
headers: What you see when it breaks

cells: Your new write is missing from the page
After a write, check the replica has caught up, else use the primary
rows.tip: Only the writer needs it. Others can see the change a little later, so it is cheap.

cells: Always send the user to the same replica
rows.tip: A single replica never goes backwards, so while you stay on one replica, time only moves forward.

marks.tip: After a write, note the leader's WAL position (LSN): the page number in the database's change log. It means "my write is at or before this page".
If the replica hasn't reached that LSN yet, this read goes to the primary, so you can't miss your own write.

blocks.title: The easy way to get monotonic reads
items: Hash on user_id in the load balancer so the same user always gets the same replica.
If that replica dies and the user moves to another, time may jump back once. That is rare enough to accept.
Checking the LSN is a small query, but don't run it on every read. Do it only when the user has written recently.
The simplest alternative: read from the primary for 5 seconds after a write. See [[data/replication/one-copy-is-risky|replication]].

items.desc: Current WAL position on the primary
How far this replica has applied the log

check.q: Which problem does always sending a user to the same replica solve?
check.a: Monotonic reads: data doesn't go backwards on refresh, because a single replica never moves back in time. It does not guarantee that you see your own writes (read-your-writes).

slides.title: Causal: the question before the answer
slides.tldr: When events depend on each other (a question and its answer), breaking their order makes users see nonsense. Causal consistency keeps it: the answer points to its cause, and a read waits for that cause.

blocks.body: Kevin asks "What time is the train?" and Ryan answers "At 9". The question and the answers sit on different shards (the data split across separate databases), and the question's copy is slow to reach this reader. The reader sees only "At 9", with no question in sight. A single-leader replica usually keeps writes in order; this situation comes from shards, multi-leader setups or separate services that take different paths.

blocks.caption: The answer arrives first, the question later

actors.label: Reader
actors.tip: Is looking at the comments page.

actors.label: Answer shard
actors.tip: Ryan's answer has already reached it.

actors.label: Question shard
actors.tip: Kevin's question is there, but hasn't reached this reader yet.

messages.note: An answer with no question: nonsense

blocks.body: The fix: the answer stores a pointer to its cause, a position in the question shard's change log (its LSN) that already contains the question. Before showing the answer, the app checks that the question shard's replica has reached that position; if not, it reads the question from the primary. The price: one extra column, one cheap query per reply, and a few reads on the primary while the replica lags. If cause and effect live in one single-leader table, skip all this: the order is already kept.

blocks.caption: With the pointer, the question is fetched before the answer is shown

actors.label: App server
actors.tip: Builds the comments page.

actors.label: Answer shard
actors.tip: Holds Ryan's answer, which carries cause_lsn.

actors.label: Question shard
actors.tip: Its replica lags a little; its primary always has the question.

messages.label: "At 9" with cause_lsn 0/5A8
messages.tip: cause_lsn is a position on the question shard that already includes Kevin's question.

messages.label: Read the question from the primary

marks.tip: The reply keeps a position on the question shard that already includes the question: its cause.
If the replica hasn't reached that position, read the question from the primary. An answer is never shown without its question.

items: Hiding replies in the browser whose parent is missing only hides the symptom. An email, an API client or a search index still gets the answer without the question.
Check once per page, not once per reply: the highest cause_lsn on the page is enough.
Some databases give causal ordering built in (MongoDB has causally consistent sessions). If yours does, use that instead.

check.q: What kind of nonsense does causal consistency prevent, and what does the answer carry to prevent it?
check.a: Seeing an effect without its cause, such as an answer without its question. The answer carries a pointer to its cause (cause_lsn), and a read waits until that cause is visible.

slides.title: A different rule for each feature
slides.tldr: Demanding strong everywhere is slow and fragile; eventual everywhere is dangerous for money. For each feature, pick the loosest rule that doesn't confuse the user.

blocks.caption: Which rule fits which feature, and how

cells: Read from the primary, inside a transaction
rows.tip: Stale means wrong decisions: spending twice or selling the same stock twice. A bit of delay is fine here.

cells: Primary after a write, or an LSN check
rows.tip: If you save and still see the old value, it looks like it didn't save. Others seeing it a bit later does no harm.
A discussion makes sense only if questions come before answers.
Slightly old is fine, but time going backwards is confusing.
Nobody notices 12 vs 13 likes. Speed matters more.

blocks.title: Three decision questions
items: Could stale data make the user or the system decide wrongly about money, stock or security?
Would the user be confused by not seeing their own write, or by time moving backwards?
If neither, eventual is fine; if so, pick the minimum rule that prevents that problem.

blocks.body: Strong for money and stock; for everything else, as loose as the user can tolerate without confusion.

use: Strong: balance, stock, unique emails, anywhere stale data causes a wrong decision
Eventual: likes, view counts, "recently viewed" lists
avoid: One rule for every feature: it is either needlessly slow or dangerous

check.q: Showing a balance versus counting likes: which needs strong and which can be eventual, and why?
check.a: The balance needs strong, because a stale value can lead to a wrong spend. Likes can be eventual: showing one or two too few harms nobody, and speed matters more.

slides.title: 51 queries on one page

slides.title: Why Doctrine runs queries silently
slides.tldr: Doctrine puts an empty proxy where a related entity should be, and the first touch fires a query. Count the queries per request and N+1 shows up.

blocks.body: When Doctrine loads an order, it doesn't load the customer. In its place it puts a **proxy**: an empty shell that knows only the id. The moment you call `getName()`, the proxy rushes off to the database. This is **lazy loading**: don't fetch until it's needed. For a single entity that's a benefit; inside a loop it is the 51 trips to the grocery store.

blocks.body: The way to bring back everything on the list in one trip is a **fetch join**: JOIN, then use `addSelect()` to tell Doctrine to build the joined entity right now. A plain `join()` changes nothing, and the customer stays a proxy. And if the page needs only three or four columns, don't build entities at all: use DQL's `NEW` to create a small **DTO** (an object that only carries data).

slides.tldr: Joining a to-many collection multiplies the rows. Instead, run a second query with `IN (…)` that loads all the collections at once: 2 queries in total.

blocks.body: Now each order has to show its items too. Items are a **collection** (to-many). Join them and 50 orders × an average of 4 items gives 200 rows, each repeating the order and customer columns. A better way is **batch loading**: fetch the orders first, then fetch all their items in one query with `IN (…)` (SQL for "any of these ids"). In shopping-list terms: two shops, two trips, not 51.

slides.tldr: With a collection fetch join, `setMaxResults(20)` applies to SQL rows, not orders. You get 5 orders instead of 20.

blocks.body: `LIMIT 20` tells the database "give me 20 **rows**", not "20 orders". Once you join the items, one order becomes 4 rows, so 20 rows yield just 5 orders, and the last order's items may even be cut off halfway. No error is raised; the page just quietly shows the wrong thing.

// I want 20 orders, but I will get 20 SQL rows

    ->addSelect('i')
    ->leftJoin('o.items', 'i')
    ->orderBy('o.createdAt', 'DESC')
    ->setMaxResults(20)
    ->getQuery()
    ->getResult();

slides.title: The monthly report started, and checkout froze
slides.tldr: Run fast little transactions and heavy reports on the same database and the report eats every resource, so customers' orders slow down.

blocks.title: The checkout counter and the monthly ledger
blocks.body: At a coffee shop's checkout counter, twenty people a minute queue up, and each one takes two seconds. If the owner sits down at that very counter and starts leafing through the whole month's receipts to add them up, the queue stops dead. Unless the counter and the accounts desk are separate, both jobs suffer.
Ryan's e-commerce app runs a sales report every night. One day the manager ran the same report at noon, and for 20 minutes every order took 8 seconds. Here are the two kinds of query side by side.

blocks.file: Two kinds of work, one database
blocks.code:
-- OLTP: 1 row, through an index, 1ms
UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 90412;

-- OLAP: reads tens of millions of rows, counts, groups
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       category_id, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY month, category_id;

marks.tip: It touches one row and it is done. A thousand of these at once won't make the database gasp.
It scans the whole table, holding CPU, memory and disk I/O for a long time.

aside.title: The manager's one click
aside.body: The report code had run safely at night for months. Nobody imagined the manager would run it at noon. The code didn't change; the time it ran did.

items.meaning: Online Transaction Processing: a huge number of small transactions such as orders, payments and logins.
Online Analytical Processing: totals, averages and trends computed across a lot of data.

check.q: Why did the manager's report slow down customers' orders, even though they use different tables?
check.a: Both share the same database server's CPU, memory and disk. The heavy scan hogged them, so the small queries had to wait.

slides.title: OLTP vs OLAP, and derived data
slides.tldr: OLTP is for small, fast reads and writes; OLAP is for big calculations. A separate copy built from the original data (the source of truth) is derived data.

blocks.body: The checkout counter is **OLTP**: countless small jobs, each touching a row or two, and the answer must be fast. The owner's accounts desk is **OLAP**: fewer jobs, but each one wades through hundreds of thousands of rows to work out a total. The original receipt book is the one and only **source of truth**. A summary copied from that book onto a separate sheet is **derived data**: if it is lost, you can rebuild it from the original.

cells: Hundreds of thousands to tens of millions
rows.tip: OLAP reads every row, but needs only a few columns.
A customer wants the answer instantly; an analyst can wait a few seconds.
In OLAP even yesterday's data is enough; the goal is to see trends.
Stored by column, `SUM(total_amount)` reads just that one column, which is much faster.

A copy or summary built from the original, such as a cache, an index or a materialized view.

check.q: Why is losing derived data cheap, while losing the source of truth is costly?
check.a: Derived data can be rebuilt from the original. If you lose the source of truth, there is nothing left to recover it from.

slides.title: Precompute summaries with a materialized view
slides.tldr: Compute the heavy query's result once and keep it like a table. Reports read the ready-made result, and the Scheduler refreshes it. The refresh itself still runs on the primary.

blocks.body: Instead of leafing through every receipt each time, the owner writes a one-page summary called "sales by month" once a night. In a database that is a **materialized view**: the query's result is actually stored on disk. A plain view is just a name, and the query inside runs every time. You can put an index on a materialized view, and `REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY` keeps reads working during the refresh. The catch: the view lives inside the primary database, and every refresh redoes the whole calculation there. The heavy query hasn't gone away; it runs once a night instead of at every report.

blocks.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW sales_by_month AS
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       category_id,
       SUM(total_amount) AS revenue,
       COUNT(*)          AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY 1, 2;

-- CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_sales_by_month
    ON sales_by_month (month, category_id);

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY sales_by_month;

marks.tip: The query's result is stored like a table. A later `SELECT` no longer recomputes anything.
Without this unique index CONCURRENTLY can't run, and a plain refresh blocks reads.
It recomputes the data and swaps it in; the old summary stays readable during the refresh.
Symfony Scheduler works like cron; you choose when the refresh runs.
The handler only refreshes. The report query is separate and reads the `sales_by_month` table.

use: The report can live with data a few minutes or an hour old
The same heavy total is needed again and again
avoid: You must show a customer their exact balance right now
The questions keep changing: a view answers only the one it was built for

items: The refresh runs the heavy query on the primary and recomputes everything, so keep it off-peak. The next slide shows a cheaper way.
MySQL has no materialized views; there you build a summary table and update it yourself.

check.q: What is the main difference between a plain view and a materialized view? Which one protects the database in reporting?
check.a: A plain view runs its query every time; a materialized view stores the result. The second does the heavy calculation once, so it protects the database.

slides.title: A view answers only the question it was built for
slides.tldr: A refresh recomputes everything on the primary, and a view serves one fixed question. A small daily summary table is cheaper to refresh and rolls up; changing questions need a warehouse.

blocks.body: The 2 a.m. refresh scans every order again. On 50 million orders that might be 5 minutes of heavy work on the primary; a year later, with 100 million, about 10. Worse, the view knows only "month and category". When the manager asks for revenue by city, per day, the view can't help, so the query goes back to the full `orders` table at noon, and checkout freezes again.

items: A refresh recomputes every row
Runs on the primary database
Answers one fixed question only
columns.tip: Simplest to set up, but each refresh redoes all the work, and the answer has one fixed shape.

columns.title: Daily summary table

A month is the sum of about 30 days
You still pick the columns in advance
columns.tip: You add only yesterday's numbers each night, so the work stays small as the table grows.

columns.title: Warehouse
items: Any slicing, any question
Heavy work leaves the primary
More to build, run and keep in step
columns.tip: A separate system built for any question, at the price of building and running it.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE sales_by_day (
    day         date    NOT NULL,
    category_id int     NOT NULL,
    revenue     numeric NOT NULL,
    orders      int     NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (day, category_id)
);

-- nightly: only yesterday's orders, found through an index on created_at
INSERT INTO sales_by_day
SELECT created_at::date, category_id, SUM(total_amount), COUNT(*)
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND created_at >= current_date - 1 AND created_at < current_date
GROUP BY 1, 2
ON CONFLICT (day, category_id)
DO UPDATE SET revenue = EXCLUDED.revenue, orders = EXCLUDED.orders;

-- a monthly report adds up about 30 small rows, not millions of orders
SELECT date_trunc('month', day) AS month, category_id, SUM(revenue)
FROM sales_by_day GROUP BY 1, 2;

marks.tip: Only yesterday's rows are read, so the nightly work follows one day of orders, not the whole table.
Running it twice for the same day just overwrites the row, so a retry is safe.
Reports read tiny rows. Days roll up into months or years; a month-only view cannot split back into days.

use: Summary table: the same few reports every day, and the orders table keeps growing
Warehouse: questions keep changing, or you need to slice by many columns
avoid: Materialized view alone, once one refresh takes minutes on the primary

items: Add an index on `orders(created_at)`, or yesterday's query scans the whole table anyway.

check.a: The view can't answer it, so the query hits the full orders table on the primary again. Add a finer summary table that includes city, or move the questions to a warehouse.

slides.title: Change data capture: let the changes travel on their own
slides.tldr: If the app writes to two places by hand, one write will eventually be missed. CDC reads the database's own log and sends the changes on, at the price of extra infrastructure and a log to watch.

blocks.body: If the app writes every order twice (once to the Primary DB, once to the reporting copy), a single failure leaves the two places disagreeing. This is called a **dual write**. The proper fix is **change data capture (CDC)**: the database itself records every change in a log (PostgreSQL's WAL). A tool such as Debezium reads that log and sends each change on to the reporting side.

marks.tip: This one succeeded.
If the server dies or the network fails here, the order exists but the copy doesn't, and nobody notices.

blocks.caption: CDC: the app writes only to the main database, and the log does the rest

nodes.label: Primary DB
nodes.tip: Every successful change is written to the log first, so the log never lies.

Old rows were never in the log, so the first run copies whole tables once: a heavy read on the primary.

items: More machinery: Debezium plus a broker such as Kafka to run, monitor and upgrade.
The log grows if the tool stops. PostgreSQL keeps the WAL until the slot has read it, so a tool that is down for a weekend can fill the primary's disk. Alert on slot lag.
The first run is a one-off snapshot of every existing row, so schedule it off-peak.
PostgreSQL needs `wal_level = logical`, and a schema change must be handled on the reporting side too.

avoid: Small apps: a nightly summary is enough, and CDC is extra hassle
Nobody can watch the log: an unwatched slot is how disks fill up

check.a: If the first write succeeds and the second fails, the two no longer match. With CDC the app writes once and the log feeds the copies, but you run extra tools and must watch the log's growth.

slides.tldr: Photos in the database bloat it. Photos on the server's disk go missing on a second server and vanish on deploy.

blocks.title: The warehouse behind the store
blocks.body: If a store owner stuffs every box of stock between the pages of the ledger, the ledger swells until it bursts. If the owner piles the boxes in one corner of the store, a new branch doesn't have the stock, and moving stores means losing it. What the owner needs is a separate warehouse; the ledger just notes "box 12, warehouse shelf 3".
In Ryan's app, a user's profile photo could be stored in two ways, and both hurt later. The code below saves the photo into the server's own `public/uploads` folder.

If two people upload the same name, one person's photo overwrites the other's.

aside.body: After a second server was added to the app, some users said their photo showed up sometimes and not other times. The load balancer was sending half the requests to the server that never had the photo.

A service that keeps files under a key (S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO).

check.a: The other server doesn't have the file, so when the load balancer sends a request there, the photo isn't found. Files must live somewhere every server can reach.

slides.title: Object storage: the database keeps only the key
slides.tldr: Files go to object storage; the database keeps the file's key and metadata. Write through Flysystem and the code survives a change of storage.

blocks.body: The box number in the warehouse is the **key**, for example `avatars/0192.../original.jpg`. The app's database holds just this key, plus the size, type and owner id. Whatever file name the user supplies, the server generates the key itself (a UUID), so nobody can overwrite anyone else's file. If you write through Symfony's **Flysystem**, it can be a local folder today and S3 tomorrow: only the config changes.

blocks.code:
flysystem:
    storages:
        uploads.storage:
            adapter: 'aws'
            options:
                client: 'aws_s3_client'   # the Aws\S3\S3Client defined in services.yaml
                bucket: '%env(S3_BUCKET)%'
                prefix: 'uploads'

marks.tip: The storage name. Autowiring's `$uploadsStorage` comes from this name.
Swap the adapter (local, aws, gcs) and the rest of the code stays the same.
The server builds the key, so a user-supplied name can't cause trouble.
`writeStream` sends the file piece by piece, so even large files don't eat much memory.

blocks.body: Keep the key in the database; keep the file in object storage.

items: Keep the bucket private by default. To show a file, use a signed URL or a CDN.
Store `avatar_key VARCHAR(255)` in the column, not the full URL; if the domain changes later, the data stays valid.

Any file your users upload
avoid: One server and a few files shipped with the app: a plain folder is simpler
Anything that must roll back with a database transaction: a file and a row are two places, so keep a pending state (see the upload slides)

check.q: What is the benefit of storing only the key, not the full file URL, in the database?
check.a: If the bucket, CDN or domain changes, the database data doesn't need to change. You build the URL from the key when you need it.

slides.title: Presigned URLs: send the file straight to storage
slides.tldr: The server mints a time-limited signed form; the Vue app POSTs the file straight to storage, with a size cap the storage itself enforces. The file never passes through your server.

blocks.body: The warehouse gate has to keep strangers out, but making every truck detour through the owner's office wastes time. So the owner hands over a signed slip good for 10 minutes (a **presigned URL**), and the truck unloads straight at the warehouse. Your PHP server never carries the weight of the file. It only grants permission, and afterwards confirms the file really arrived. The slip can also say "no box heavier than 5 MB". That needs a presigned **POST** with a policy: a presigned PUT can't cap the size.

blocks.code:
<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref } from 'vue'
const progress = ref(0)

async function upload(file: File) {
  const res = await fetch('/uploads/presign', { method: 'POST' })
  const { key, url, fields } = await res.json()

  const form = new FormData()
  for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(fields)) form.append(name, value as string)
  form.append('file', file)   // the file field must come last

  await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => {
    const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest()
    xhr.open('POST', url)
    xhr.upload.onprogress = (e) => (progress.value = Math.round((e.loaded / e.total) * 100))
    xhr.onload = () => (xhr.status < 300 ? resolve() : reject(new Error('upload failed')))
    xhr.onerror = () => reject(new Error('network'))
    xhr.send(form)
  })
  await fetch('/uploads/confirm', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ key }),
  })
}
</script>

marks.tip: Storage reads the form top to bottom. Every field from the server goes first, the file last.
`fetch` can't report upload progress, but `XMLHttpRequest` can, so it is used here.

check.a: The policy makes storage refuse oversize files up front. The check afterwards proves the file really arrived with the right type, because the client's "done" can be wrong or a lie.

slides.title: Confirm or clean up: no upload left behind
slides.tldr: A client can fetch a URL and never upload, or upload and vanish before confirming. Record every upload as pending, promote it only after the server's own check, and delete whatever stays pending.

blocks.body: Every presigned URL is a promise the client may break. Some users get a URL and close the tab. Others upload the file, then lose the connection before calling confirm. Either way, objects pile up in the bucket with no database row pointing at them, and you pay for them forever. The fix: write a `pending` row the moment you mint the URL, let confirm check the object and flip the row to `uploaded`, and have a scheduled job delete whatever is still pending after an hour.

check.a: The pending row made when the URL was minted. The hourly job finds it still pending and deletes both the row and the object.

slides.title: Large files: in pieces, and resumable
slides.tldr: Send a big file in one go and a dropped connection means starting over. Multipart upload splits it into parts, and only the failed part is resent.

blocks.body: Send a 2 GB video in a single request, lose the connection at 90%, and everything is wasted. Just as a big shipment reaches the warehouse split into small boxes, **multipart upload** cuts the file into parts of 5 to 100 MB. Each part goes to its own URL, and at the end you say "all parts have arrived" and they are stitched together. A failed part can simply be sent again, and the next slide shows how to carry on after a crash.

slides.title: One renamed field broke the mobile app
slides.tldr: Change the shape (schema) of an API or message and every reader that expects the old shape breaks. Both sides never deploy at the same moment, so changes must be made carefully.

blocks.title: The courier's form
blocks.body: Imagine a courier office quietly renames the "Phone" box on its form to "Mobile". A clerk holding an old form can't find the box, and the parcel gets stuck. The people who print the forms and the people who read them are different, and they switch at different times. So any change has to leave both the old and the new form readable.

Ryan's team renamed `phone` to `mobile` in an API response. The web app was fixed the same day, but the old mobile app sitting in the Play Store would keep looking for `phone` for another two weeks. During that gap it showed an empty number.

aside.body: Plenty of users go months without updating an app. On the day your server changes, old versions are still out there running. Changing an API's shape is like walking into a house that is half renovated.

slides.title: JSON, Protobuf, Avro: how each one writes data
slides.tldr: JSON is human-readable but bulky; Protobuf and Avro are compact and schema-driven. Protobuf identifies fields by number, while Avro carries the writer's schema alongside.

blocks.body: Picture three ways to write a letter: full sentences in plain language (JSON), short codes keyed to box numbers on a form (Protobuf), or a letter with a page attached that lists what each box means (Avro). JSON writes every field name into every message, so it's big. Protobuf sends a **field number** (`= 1`, `= 2`) instead of a name, so it's small, and that number is the field's real identity. Avro data carries no names at all; to read it you need the schema it was written with.

blocks.caption: The three formats side by side

rows.tip: Binary formats don't repeat field names in every message.
JSON is the easiest to debug; binary formats need tooling.
With a schema, a compiler or registry catches breaking changes early.
In Protobuf, renaming a field is safe and changing its number is disastrous.
Counted for order_id 9001, total_amount 2500, currency USD. The binary formats leave out every field name, which is where most of the saving comes from.
Each has its place; for browsers, JSON is almost always the answer.

marks.tip: On the wire this travels as `1: <value>`. The name `order_id` is never sent, so changing the number turns it into a different field.

aside.body: In JSON the name is the identity; in Protobuf the number is.

items.meaning: The bytes exactly as they travel between two machines, as opposed to the objects inside your program.

use: JSON: browser-facing APIs, or when easy debugging matters
Protobuf/Avro: huge message volumes between services, where small size and a strict schema are needed
avoid: Picking a binary format only because it sounds "fast"; measure first

check.q: In Protobuf, renaming a field is safe but changing its number is not. Why?
check.a: Names never go over the wire, only numbers do. Change a number and old data is either not recognized (the value is lost) or read as a different field.

slides.title: Safe changes: adding, removing and renaming fields
slides.tldr: Add new fields as optional or with a default. Stop using a field before you remove it. A rename is an add, then a later remove of the old one.

blocks.body: The goal is that both the old and the new shape stay readable. The rules are simple. **Adding** a field is safe if a reader that doesn't find it falls back to a default. **Removing** a field is safe only once nobody reads it anymore. A **rename** is really an add and a remove, done in two separate steps. Symfony Messenger queues hold old messages for a while, so the same rules apply there.

marks.tip: Even if v1 messages are still sitting in the queue, the object can be built without this field because it has a default.
`?string` with a `null` default: "absent" is a valid state.

framework:

        serializer:
            default_serializer: messenger.transport.symfony_serializer
            symfony_serializer:

# Not PHP's native serialize(): old messages become hard to read once the class changes

marks.tip: With JSON messages, everything except a class rename is easy to handle, and consumers in other languages can read them too.

Old readers ignore the new field

Old senders don't send the field, so new readers fail.

rows.tip: Check logs or metrics to confirm nobody still reads it.

rows.tip: Sending the data under both names keeps both kinds of reader working.
Going from `int` to `string` breaks every reader. Add a new field under a new name instead.

items: Loosen strict validation in consumers: ignore unknown fields. That is the tolerant reader.
A `version` field or header in a public API makes it easier to tell which readers are affected during a change.

check.q: What steps would you take to move the `phone` field to the name `mobile`?
check.a: First add `mobile` and send both fields. Once every reader has switched to the new one, remove `phone`.

slides.title: The trap of reused numbers and required fields
slides.tldr: Reuse the number or name of a removed field and old data gets read with the wrong meaning. Use reserved to forbid it.

blocks.body: The `phone` field (a string, number 4) was removed. A few months later someone gives the same number 4 to a new string field, `coupon_code`. But old messages are still on disk or in a queue, and in them 4 holds a phone number. The new reader will happily treat "555-0101" as a coupon code, with no error at all. It's a mistake of meaning, not of spelling, which makes it the most dangerous kind.

marks.tip: In old messages, 4 holds a phone number. Read as `coupon_code`, it is a plausible-looking string, so nothing complains and the wrong value flows on.
With `reserved`, the compiler refuses to let that number or name be used again. The mistake is caught before deploy.

blocks.body: Never reuse the number or name of a removed field.

items: Adding a new required field makes messages from old senders get rejected. This is why proto3 dropped `required`.
If the new field had a different type (an int32), old string data would be dropped instead of misread. Still wrong, only quieter; `reserved` guards against both.
When you add a new enum value, old readers don't recognize it; decide up front what they should do with an unknown value.

aside.body: Bury a field number; never resurrect it.

check.q: What do you gain by writing `reserved` for a removed field's number?
check.a: If someone later gives that number or name to a new field, the compiler errors immediately. Old data can't be read with the wrong meaning.

slides.title: Schema registry: the guardian of changes
slides.tldr: A schema registry stores every schema version, checks compatibility before a new schema is accepted, and messages carry only a schema id.

blocks.body: When many teams share one queue or Kafka topic, any of them can change a schema without asking the others. A **schema registry** is a central ledger that stores every version of every schema. When you submit a new version, it first checks whether it fits with the old ones. If it doesn't, the registry refuses it, so a breaking schema can't reach production. Instead of embedding the whole schema in each message, the message carries just a small **schema id**.

blocks.code:
v1  order_id, total_amount, currency
v2  + coupon_code, required, no default  -> REJECTED: v2 cannot read v1 messages
v2  + coupon_code, default null          -> accepted: v1 messages still readable

marks.tip: Old messages have no coupon_code, so a reader on this schema would have nothing to fill the required field with. The registry refuses the schema before any message is sent.

items: **BACKWARD**: the new schema can read old messages (consumers upgrade first).
**FORWARD**: the old schema can read new messages (producers upgrade first).
**FULL**: both. The safest choice between teams that don't know each other.
The price: one more service to run and keep available. Clients cache schemas, but a registry that is down blocks new schemas from being registered.
The idea works even without a registry: keep schema files in git and run a compatibility check in CI (for example `buf breaking`).

items.meaning: A service that stores every version of a schema and checks compatibility.
A small number sent with each message that identifies one schema version in the registry.

check.q: Which risk grows without a registry, and how does a registry reduce it?
check.a: Anyone can release a breaking schema without telling anyone. The registry checks compatibility before accepting a schema, so a broken one is stopped.

slides.title: One ALTER TABLE froze the whole site
slides.tldr: A schema-change command on a big table holds a lock while every query behind it queues up. New code running against an old schema breaks things too.

blocks.title: Replacing a bridge on a busy road
blocks.body: Close a busy highway to demolish its old bridge and hundreds of thousands of people are stuck. A sensible engineer builds a new bridge alongside, moves the traffic onto it, and only then tears down the old one. A database schema change works the same way: don't tear down the old structure in place; build the new one next to it and move across step by step.

At midday, Ryan ran a migration that changed a column on the `users` table, which has 10 million rows. The command held a lock on the table for 40 seconds, a lock that blocks all reads and writes. At 100 requests a second, that is 4,000 queries piled up behind it, and a connection pool of 50 is full within the first second.

actors.label: Database

blocks.body: Write every migration on the assumption that the site stays up while it runs.

aside.title: Old code, new schema
aside.body: There's a second kind of trouble. The migration finishes, but half the servers are still running old code, which looks for a column that's gone. Deploys don't happen all at once; for a while, old and new code and schema coexist.

items.meaning: Users notice no interruption while the change is being made.
A lock that stops everyone else from reading or writing that table while it is held.

check.a: While ALTER holds the lock, every query on that table queues up and the connection pool fills. Then even unrelated pages can't respond.

slides.title: Expand, migrate, contract: build the bridge alongside
slides.tldr: Three safe steps: first add the new structure (expand), then move data and code over (migrate), and finally remove the old one (contract). Each step is its own deploy.

blocks.body: To rename the `phone` column to `mobile_number`, you can't run `RENAME COLUMN` in one go, because old code will still look for `phone` while the deploy rolls out. So it takes three phases. **Expand**: add the new column and keep the old one. **Migrate**: make the code write to both columns, copy the old data into the new one, then switch reads to the new column. **Contract**: once nothing uses the old column, drop it. At the end of every step, both old and new code can run.
