check.a: During the deploy, old code still looks for `phone`, which no longer exists. Splitting it into add, move and drop avoids this.

slides.title: The expand step in a Doctrine Migration
slides.tldr: Write Doctrine Migrations with a nullable column, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `lock_timeout`. Locks stay short, and a failure backs out quickly.

blocks.body: In PostgreSQL, adding a nullable column with a default is nearly instant. But a plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks writes to the table, while `CONCURRENTLY` doesn't, though it can't run inside a transaction. So in Doctrine Migrations you return `false` from `isTransactional()`. Even a change that takes a millisecond must first wait for every running query on the table to finish, and all new queries queue behind it. So set a `lock_timeout`: if the lock isn't available, the migration gives up after 3 seconds instead of freezing the site.

marks.tip: Without a transaction, a failure halfway leaves the work half done, so keep a migration like this small.
If the lock isn't available, it errors out after 3 seconds. Let the migration fail rather than the site, and run it again later.
CONCURRENTLY builds the index without locking the table. It takes longer, but writes keep flowing.
Writing both columns means that even after a rollback, old code finds correct data.
Rows not yet backfilled have an empty `mobileNumber`, hence the fallback.

items: If `CONCURRENTLY` fails it leaves an INVALID index behind. Run `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and build it again.
In MySQL, spell out `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE`; if that's not possible it errors instead of quietly taking a lock.

items.desc: generate a migration from your entities, then review it by hand
see the SQL without running it
see which migrations are still pending

check.q: If you run a migration with `lock_timeout = 3s` and the lock isn't available, what happens, and why is that good?
check.a: After 3 seconds the migration errors out by itself. The site doesn't freeze, and you can rerun the failed migration in a quiet period.

slides.title: Backfill: millions of rows in small batches
slides.tldr: One `UPDATE` over 10 million rows means a long lock and a huge transaction. Instead, run a re-runnable command that handles 1,000 rows at a time with a short pause.

blocks.body: Updating 10 million rows in one `UPDATE` means minutes of locking, a gigantic transaction log, and replicas falling behind. A better approach is like cooking for a large catered event: not every pot at once, but one at a time. Process 1,000 rows per round, pause briefly between rounds, and advance by `id` so that if it stops partway you can restart from the same place. The price is total time: at about 0.06 s of work plus a 0.1 s pause per 1,000 rows, 10 million rows take around 27 minutes. That is fine, because it runs in the background and nobody waits for it.

marks.tip: Advancing with `id > ?` resumes from the last position each time. Because of `mobile_number IS NULL`, a rerun never touches rows already done.
A short pause. It keeps replicas from lagging and leaves room for other queries.

blocks.caption: 10 million rows: how long one transaction holds its locks

items.label: One UPDATE
items.tip: The rows stay locked for that long, and the transaction log grows huge too.

items.label: 10,000 per batch
items.tip: Much better, but a lock this long can still make a busy page stutter at peak hours.

items.label: 1,000 per batch
items.tip: Each batch is so short that no query gets stuck behind it. (The time per row is the same as in the single UPDATE: 10 minutes for 10 million rows.)

items: Add a `--dry-run` option that reports how many rows are left; it also gives you progress while the job runs.
Measure replica lag (how far behind the copy servers fall). If lag grows, shrink the batch size or lengthen the pause.
Advance with `id >`, not OFFSET; OFFSET gets slower as rows pile up and can skip rows when data changes underneath it.

check.q: If the backfill command is stopped halfway and you run it again, what happens, and why is that safe?
check.a: Rows whose `mobile_number` is already filled are excluded by the `IS NULL` condition, so only the remaining ones are picked up. The job is idempotent and can be rerun freely.

slides.title: Traps: NOT NULL, foreign keys and plain indexes
slides.tldr: On a big table, a direct `SET NOT NULL`, `ADD FOREIGN KEY` or plain `CREATE INDEX` scans or locks the whole table. Doing it in two steps (NOT VALID, then VALIDATE) is safe.

blocks.body: The new column will eventually need `NOT NULL`, but a direct `SET NOT NULL` scans the whole table and holds a lock while it does. Foreign keys behave the same way. The fix: first add the constraint as **NOT VALID** (only new writes are checked, not existing rows), then run a separate `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, which doesn't block the table. The price: more steps, and if `VALIDATE` finds a bad row it fails. Fix the data and run it again; nothing broke meanwhile. A plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks writes, so use `CONCURRENTLY`, as on the previous slides.

marks.tip: On a big table this can take minutes, and writes are blocked the whole time.
A plain CREATE INDEX lets reads through but blocks all writes to the table for as long as the build takes.
With `NOT VALID`, only new writes are checked right now; existing rows aren't examined, so the lock stays short.
`VALIDATE` takes a weaker lock: reads and writes continue.
From PostgreSQL 12, with a valid CHECK constraint in place, `SET NOT NULL` skips the scan.
The foreign key gets the same treatment: add it NOT VALID, then VALIDATE while traffic carries on.

blocks.body: On a big table, any command that scans every row also holds a lock. Take the short lock first, do the heavy check later.

items: Dropping a column comes dead last: if old code still reads it, you get 500 errors immediately.
Changing a column's type (`ALTER TYPE`) often rewrites the whole table. Build a new column and use expand-contract.
On a table with only a few thousand rows, a direct `SET NOT NULL` finishes in milliseconds. The two-step path is for big, busy tables.

aside.body: On big tables: NOT VALID first, VALIDATE after.

check.q: Why use `CHECK ... NOT VALID` and `VALIDATE` instead of a direct `SET NOT NULL`?
check.a: A direct statement holds the lock for the whole table scan. Two steps keep the lock short, and writes aren't blocked while validation runs.

slides.title: The price changed, and so did the old invoices
slides.tldr: UPDATE wipes out the old value, so you can't answer "what was it before?", "who changed it?" or "which price applied then?".

blocks.title: The store's account book
blocks.body: When there's a mistake in the account book, a sensible store owner doesn't scratch it out. The owner writes a new line: "Correction: $5 less, date, signature". In a scratched-out book nobody can tell what was written before. UPDATE is exactly that scratching out: the old value is gone, and so is who changed it and why.

At Ryan's shop, the price of rice went from 80 to $90. Someone ran `UPDATE products SET price = 90 WHERE id = 7`. The invoice page reads the price from `products`, so last week's invoice now shows $90, and the customer says, "But I bought it at 80." There's no proof either way.

blocks.caption: The same event: overwriting vs keeping history

columns.title: UPDATE only
items: The invoice now says $90
Who changed it? Unknown
What was last month's price? Unknown
columns.tip: The table holds only the current state. The database knows nothing about the past.

columns.title: Keeping history
items: The invoice shows the $80 from the time of sale
Who, when and why are all recorded
The price on any date can be looked up
columns.tip: Every step of a change is stored as its own row.

blocks.file: invoice query: the same line before and after

marks.tip: The join reads whatever the price is now. After the UPDATE to 90, every old invoice silently shows 90.
unit_price is written once and never joined back to products. A later price change cannot touch it.

blocks.body: If a value might ever be questioned, don't overwrite it. Add a new line.

aside.title: Who raised the salary?
aside.body: An audit found that an employee's salary had changed three times, but the table held only the last figure. Who changed it, when, and with whose approval? No answers. An app may have a "last updated" column, but it never keeps the previous value.

items: Copying the price answers "what did this customer pay?". It can't answer "what was the price on 10 February?" for a product nobody bought that day; that needs effective dating (slide 3).

items.meaning: An unalterable list of who changed what, and when.
Data that changes over time, where you also need to know its past states.

check.q: What are two different ways to keep an old invoice's price correct?
check.a: Copy the price into `order_items` at the time of sale (a snapshot), or keep a price history and look up which price applied on that date.

slides.title: Audit history: who changed what, and when
slides.tldr: Every important change adds a new row to an audit table: who, when, which record, the old and new values. Rows are never changed or deleted.

blocks.body: An audit table follows the ledger's rule: lines are only ever added, and nobody touches the old ones. Each row records **who** (the actor), **when**, **which** record, what action, and the old and new values. It has to be written in the same transaction as the main change: if the change succeeds the audit row exists, and if it fails both disappear. Written separately, a crash between the two would leave a price change with no record of who made it.

blocks.code:
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    actor_id    BIGINT,              -- NULL = system / console command
    entity_type VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    entity_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
    action      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, -- created | updated | deleted
    old_values  JSONB,
    new_values  JSONB
);
CREATE INDEX idx_audit_entity ON audit_log (entity_type, entity_id, occurred_at);

marks.tip: NULL means no user was involved, such as a cron job or console command. You need to know that too.
Almost every question is "show me this record's history", so the index follows that order.
`wrapInTransaction` commits or rolls back the main change and the audit row together.
Both the old and the new value: without knowing "what it was", the history is incomplete.

blocks.title: Rules for the audit table
items: INSERT only: don't grant the app's database user UPDATE or DELETE.
Store the actor's id, not just the name (names change).
Never put secrets like passwords or card numbers in old/new values.

A database trigger catches every change, even hand-typed SQL, but it doesn't know the app user unless you pass it (for example SET LOCAL app.user_id). Writing from the app knows the user but misses anything done outside it.
An audit log is not an application log. App logs get rotated away; audit data is legal evidence.
The table only grows, one row per change. Plan how long to keep it, and partition it by month once it gets big.

items.label: How long to keep audit data

check.q: Why must the audit row be written in the same transaction as the main change?
check.a: If the change happens but the audit row doesn't (or the reverse), the history has a gap or false information. In one transaction, both succeed or both fail.

slides.title: Effective dating: which price on which date
slides.tldr: Each price row has `valid_from` and `valid_to`. One query answers "what was the price on 10 February?", and an exclusion constraint prevents overlapping periods.

blocks.body: An audit says who changed something and when; **effective dating** says which value was valid during which period. In a price table you don't edit a row. You close the old row's `valid_to` and add a new row. An empty `valid_to` means "still in force". You can even set a price for a future date, such as a Black Friday offer starting on a set date. Without a guard, one typo can leave two rows covering 20 February, so the lookup returns two prices and nobody knows which is right. An exclusion constraint in PostgreSQL stops that.

blocks.code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

CREATE TABLE product_prices (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    product_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES products (id),
    amount     INT NOT NULL CHECK (amount >= 0),
    valid_from TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    valid_to   TIMESTAMPTZ,            -- NULL = still in force
    EXCLUDE USING gist (
        product_id WITH =,
        (tstzrange(valid_from, valid_to)) WITH &&
    )
);

-- Which price applied at noon on 10 February?
SELECT amount FROM product_prices
WHERE product_id = 7
  AND valid_from <= '2026-02-10 12:00-05'
  AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to > '2026-02-10 12:00-05');

marks.tip: Two rows for the same product can never have overlapping periods. The database itself blocks the mistake.
It started at or before `t`, and either hasn't ended or ends after `t`: these two conditions match exactly one row.
The old row isn't deleted; it only gets a `valid_to`. The history stays intact.

blocks.caption: Price history for product 7

rows.tip: Purchases made during this period were at $80.
An empty `valid_to` means this is the current price.

aside.body: Don't edit the row; close the old one and open a new one.

items: Copying the price onto the invoice line is the simplest approach. Effective dating pays off when you regularly need to know "what was it on that date".

check.q: Two rows for the same product in the price table could end up with overlapping periods. How do you prevent that in the database?
check.a: In PostgreSQL, use an `EXCLUDE USING gist` constraint that rejects a row when the `product_id` matches and the time ranges overlap.

slides.title: Soft delete: the convenience and the traps
slides.tldr: Soft delete means setting `deleted_at`. But unique constraints get in the way, and forgetting the filter in one query shows deleted data. The fixes are a partial unique index and a Doctrine filter.

blocks.body: **Soft delete** means keeping the row and setting `deleted_at`, so that an accidental delete can be undone and history stays. **Hard delete** really removes the row. The first trap: `users.email` is unique. Ryan deletes his account and tries to sign up again with the same email, but the deleted row is still holding that email, so he gets a unique error. The second trap: forget `deleted_at IS NULL` in even one query and deleted users reappear.

marks.tip: A partial unique index: uniqueness is only required among the rows that match the `WHERE` condition.
`lower(email)` makes the check case-insensitive.
Doctrine adds this condition to the WHERE of every query itself. Nobody can forget it.
For entities without a `deletedAt` field, the filter adds nothing.

blocks.caption: Soft delete or hard delete

columns.title: Soft delete
items: Accidental deletes can be undone
History and references stay intact
Needs a filter and a partial unique index
Personal data isn't really erased
columns.tip: Use it when you need to undo deletes and keep history. But personal data stays behind.

columns.title: Hard delete
items: The data is truly gone
Can cause foreign key trouble
Can't be undone (without a backup)
columns.tip: For when data really must go, such as privacy requests or expired data.

items: To show or restore deleted rows (an admin screen), switch the filter off for that request: `$em->getFilters()->disable('soft_delete')`.
Native SQL and reporting queries don't get the Doctrine filter. There you must write `deleted_at IS NULL` by hand.
Soft delete makes the database grow; run a hard-delete job 30 to 90 days after deletion.

items.label: When to really remove deleted data

check.q: Signing up again with a soft-deleted email gives a unique error. How do you fix it?
check.a: Drop the column-wide unique constraint and create a partial unique index with `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. Then uniqueness applies only to live rows.

slides.title: "Delete my data" and the hidden copies
slides.tldr: A user's data isn't only in the users table: copies live in logs, backups, search, analytics and caches. Skip lifecycle planning and deletion becomes nearly impossible.

blocks.title: Old papers around the house
blocks.body: Bills, letters and deeds pile up in a home year after year. The house deed must be kept for life, utility bills for a few years, and the grocery list can go straight in the bin. If nobody decides how long each kind stays, everything sits in one heap, and on the day you need something you can't find it.

A user who signed up five years ago writes, "Delete all my information." Ryan runs `DELETE FROM users` and thinks he's done. But that person's email and phone number are scattered across other places: the logs, the search index, the analytics warehouse, the backups, and in a real system more.

blocks.caption: How many places one user's data spreads to

nodes.label: users table
nodes.tip: Where we think of deleting. In reality it is just one of the copies.

nodes.label: App logs
nodes.tip: An email or phone number gets written to a log by mistake and piles up for years.

nodes.label: Search index
nodes.tip: A separate copy; it isn't deleted automatically along with the users table.

nodes.label: Analytics
nodes.tip: Data copied for reporting; names or ids may be in here too.

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.tip: Like a photograph, frozen in time; old backups still contain the user.

edges.label: Requests write the email into the logs
Name and email get copied into the search index
A copy, with history, goes to the warehouse
A backup of everything is taken every night

blocks.body: Decide how long you keep data, why, and how you'll delete it on the day you collect it.

aside.title: The old data that leaked
aside.body: A small service had a data breach. Most of the leaked records belonged to users who had left four years earlier, whose data was no use to anyone. Had it not been kept, there would have been no harm.

items.meaning: The life of data from birth to death: collection, use, storage, archiving, deletion.
A user's right to have their personal data erased (the erasure right in GDPR).

check.q: Why does a user's data survive a `DELETE FROM users`?
check.a: It also lives as separate copies in logs, the search index, analytics, backups and caches. Deleting the main table doesn't remove the copies.

slides.title: Retention policy and data minimization
slides.tldr: For each kind of data, write down in advance why you keep it, for how long, and what happens afterwards. And collect only what you truly need from the start.

blocks.body: Like those old papers, each kind of data needs a rule: a **retention policy**. It says why you keep it (the purpose), for how long, and what happens at the end (delete or archive). The second rule is **data minimization**: don't ask for information you don't really need. Data you never collected can't leak and never has to be deleted. Some data you must keep by law, such as payment records. You can't delete it, but you can strip away the person's identity.

blocks.caption: A sample retention policy (the numbers are examples; set yours by your law and business)

rows.tip: The purpose is narrow, so the period is short. After an investigation, this data has no further use.
The law sets this period; deleting earlier would break the law.
Keeping it a while after closure lets you undo an accidental account closure.
The proof of when someone consented is data too; delete it when its time is up.

blocks.title: Data minimization: three questions before you collect
items: Can we provide the service without this information? If so, don't take it.
Do we need the full date of birth, or is an age check enough?
When will this stop being useful? Write that date down now.
Keep the policy in code, not on paper: the number of days in `config/retention.yaml`, and a job that follows it.
Keep a list of which columns hold personal data (PII); otherwise, what will you delete?
Laws differ by country and by type of data. Alongside GDPR and the laws that apply where you operate, get advice from your company's lawyer; the numbers here are only samples.

check.q: The law says order records must be kept for 7 years, but the user asks you to delete their data. What do you do?
check.a: Keep the accounting row but anonymize the personal data (name, email, address). The legal record survives, and the person can't be identified.

slides.title: Purge jobs and archives: deleting by the rules
slides.tldr: Delete expired data nightly through the Scheduler, in small batches. For data you occasionally need, archive it to cheap storage first, verify, then delete.

blocks.body: Old papers get thrown out on a schedule, with one big clear-out a year. A database needs a **purge job** that runs at 3:30am and removes rows whose retention period has passed. On a big table, don't delete millions of rows at once, because of locks and replica lag. Delete in small batches, just like a [[data/zero-downtime-migrations/alter-table-freeze|backfill]]. Some data may be needed years later; archive that first.

marks.tip: The retention period isn't hard-coded; it comes from a parameter. When the policy changes, you change the config.
PostgreSQL has no `DELETE ... LIMIT`, so a subquery picks 5,000 ids.
Keep going while a full batch gets deleted. A smaller count means nothing is left.

blocks.caption: The safe order for archive-then-delete

steps.title: 1. Select
steps.body: Pick the expired rows
steps.tip: Rows older than the cutoff date, in batches by id.

steps.title: 2. Archive
steps.body: As files in cheap storage
steps.tip: Parquet or CSV in object storage, in year-month folders.

steps.title: 3. Verify
steps.body: Match row counts and checksums
steps.tip: Deleting without verifying what was written to the archive is dangerous.

steps.title: 4. Delete
steps.body: Remove from the main table
steps.tip: Only after verification passes, and in small batches.

items: If you partition the table by date, dropping or detaching an old partition is the deletion: instant, and no heavy DELETE.
Record how many rows each purge deleted in a metric or log; a sudden zero or a huge number signals a problem.
Compute the cutoff from `ClockInterface`, not the current time directly; then tests can set the time and check the result.

check.q: Why does a purge job delete in batches of 5,000 instead of running one `DELETE`?
check.a: One huge DELETE holds a long lock, bloats the transaction log and makes replicas fall behind. Small batches keep each lock brief, so the site keeps running.

slides.title: Erasure: delete, anonymize, and tell the copies
slides.tldr: For an account-deletion request, anonymize personal data while keeping legal records, tell every copy with an event, and keep an erasure list for backups.

blocks.body: Deleting the row breaks foreign keys and loses the order accounts. So you usually **anonymize**: replace the name, email and phone with meaningless values, but keep the order rows and the money amounts. Then publish a `UserErased` event so that search, analytics and cache clean up their own copies. Keep a separate list of who was erased, stored **outside** the database you back up and restore: a restore would bring the erased user back, and it would roll back an in-database list too.

marks.tip: The row stays (foreign keys intact), but nobody can recognize it as a person anymore.
The list lives in a separate database, so a restore of the main one cannot roll it back. With it, you can anonymize everyone again after the restore.
Dispatch the event after the transaction ends, otherwise an event for a failed transaction might go out.

blocks.caption: The person's data vs the legal record

columns.title: Anonymize
items: Order and invoice rows
Remove name, email, phone, address
Money amounts and dates stay
columns.tip: For data where you need the row for accounts or statistics but don't need to know who the person is.

columns.title: Delete completely
items: Profile pictures, files
Copies in the search index and cache
Marketing lists and device tokens
columns.tip: Data you have no legal reason to keep should be removed entirely.

blocks.body: To delete, remove every copy, not just the main table. And keep a list of erased users for backups.

items: Never write emails or phone numbers into app logs. Deleting from logs is almost impossible, so log the user id from the start.
If a `UserErased` event is lost, copies survive; look at the outbox pattern to guarantee delivery.

Rows can't be removed from inside a backup; a backup simply expires after its retention period. After a restore, re-run the anonymization from `erasure_log`, which must live outside the restored database.

check.q: After a user asks to be deleted, a backup restore brings their data back. What should you have kept to prevent it?
check.a: An `erasure_log` of erased users, stored outside the restored database. After the restore, run the anonymization again from that list, and the data doesn't come back.

slides.title: Last month's sales: three departments, three numbers
slides.tldr: When everyone copies the data and does their own sums, one question gets three answers. A data platform means one place, one definition, one set of rules.

blocks.title: Warehouses scattered around town
blocks.body: Three sellers of the same product each count their own stock in their own shop; one subtracts returns, another doesn't. Ask the owner and you get three numbers. The fix is one central warehouse, the same counting rules for everybody, and a name on every shelf saying who looks after it.

At Ryan's company, someone asked for last month's sales. Finance said $420,000, Marketing said 4,500,000, and the product database gave 4,000,000. Nobody made a mistake. Each counted at a different time, from a different copy, with a different definition.

blocks.caption: The real reason for the three numbers

rows.tip: Counted the money actually received, with refunds subtracted.
Counted at the moment of ordering without subtracting refunds, so the figure is higher.
The time zone and the copy's date differ, so the month boundary shifted.

blocks.body: One metric, one definition, one owner, one place.

aside.title: The board meeting numbers
aside.body: At a board meeting, two directors showed different customer counts. Half the meeting went on reconciling the numbers. Nobody could decide anything, because nobody knew which number to trust.

items.meaning: A business number, like "monthly sales", that has one fixed definition.
An automated path that takes data from one place and moves it, step by step, to another.

check.q: Finance and Marketing gave different numbers and neither made a mistake. Why didn't they match?
check.a: They counted from different copies with different definitions: refunds in or out, different time boundaries. Without one definition and one source, the numbers won't agree.

slides.title: Warehouse, lake, lakehouse: three kinds of storehouse
slides.tldr: A warehouse is a tidy store of clean data; a lake is a huge reservoir of raw data of every kind; a lakehouse tries to bring the strengths of both into one place.

blocks.body: A **warehouse** is a storehouse with labeled shelves: data is cleaned first and arranged into defined tables, so SQL reports are fast and reliable. A **lake** is like a grain silo: images, logs, JSON and CSV are dumped as they are into cheap object storage and read later as needed. It's cheap, but without tidiness it turns into a "data swamp". A **lakehouse** puts shelf labels on top of the silo (Parquet, Delta Lake and Iceberg formats), so SQL runs directly on the same files.

blocks.caption: The three compared

rows.tip: A lakehouse often keeps three layers called raw, cleaned and curated.
Schema on write catches mistakes early; schema on read is flexible but catches them late.
Lakes and lakehouses use object storage, which is much cheaper.
Data science wants raw data and BI wants clean data; a lakehouse gives both teams one place.
For a small team, a PostgreSQL replica or a managed warehouse is often enough.

blocks.title: Which one, and when
items: First step: for a small app a read replica or a separate PostgreSQL is enough; don't reach for big-data tools in advance.
When reports and dashboards multiply, use a managed warehouse.
When you need raw logs, images or ML, use a lake or lakehouse.

aside.body: Warehouse = tidy shelves, lake = grain silo, lakehouse = shelf labels on the silo.

items.label: Why reports belong in a separate place

check.q: You want to keep images, logs and JSON files together cheaply and analyze them later as needed. Which fits?
check.a: A data lake. All the raw data can be kept as it is in object storage, and the schema is decided at read time. For tidy SQL reports, use a warehouse.

slides.title: The ELT pipeline: bring it in first, cook in the warehouse
slides.tldr: With ELT, raw data goes into the warehouse first (Extract, Load), then SQL cleans and shapes it there (Transform). Symfony extracts to a file in the lake and the warehouse loads that file into the raw layer.

blocks.body: In old-style **ETL**, you bought goods at the grocery store and cooked them at home before putting them in the warehouse. In modern **ELT**, the raw goods go straight into the warehouse, and the cooking happens on its big stove (the warehouse's SQL). The benefits: raw data stays intact, and if the cooking rules change you can cook again. Symfony does the first two steps. It picks up changed rows using a **watermark** (a marker for how far we got), writes them as a file in the lake, then tells the warehouse to load that file into the raw layer. The watermark moves only after the load succeeds, so a crash can cause duplicates, never lost rows.

blocks.caption: The warehouse's three layers: from raw to business-ready

layers.label: mart: mart_daily_sales
layers.sub: Answers business questions; dashboards read from here
layers.tip: Shaped for the owner. Definitions are settled here, and everyone reads this table.

layers.label: staging: stg_orders
layers.sub: Duplicates removed, names and types fixed
layers.tip: Raw data gets cleaned in this layer; the latest row is picked.

layers.label: raw: raw_orders
layers.tip: Never modified. Every loaded file lands here, and if something goes wrong you can rebuild from here.

marks.tip: With `>=`, rows with the same timestamp come again. Some duplicates will arrive, but no row gets lost (at-least-once).
It reads from a read replica, not the transactional database, so the OLTP side isn't put under load.
The load is a bulk file copy by the warehouse itself, not row-by-row inserts from PHP. If it throws, the watermark stays put.
The watermark moves only after the file is written and loaded. If anything fails midway, the next run starts from the same place.

blocks.code:
-- run once: the raw layer keeps every row exactly as extracted
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS raw.raw_orders (
  id           INT64,
  user_id      INT64,
  total_amount NUMERIC,
  status       STRING,
  created_at   TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at   TIMESTAMP
);

-- what the command runs for each file; JSON keys match the column names
LOAD DATA INTO raw.raw_orders
FROM FILES (
  format = 'JSON',
  uris = ['gs://shop-lake/raw/orders/dt=2026-03-01/0192-example.jsonl']
);

marks.tip: Both timestamps are kept: `created_at` says which day the sale belongs to, `updated_at` picks the newest version of a row.
It appends. Loading the same file twice gives duplicate rows, which the staging layer removes on the next slide.

items: Every warehouse has a native bulk load: BigQuery `LOAD DATA`, Snowflake and Redshift `COPY`. Use it instead of inserting rows one by one.
Keep ELT steps idempotent in effect: running one twice gives the same final result. Then rerunning is the fix when something fails.
Rows that were DELETEd can't be caught by `updated_at`. Use soft delete, or CDC.

check.q: The load fails after the file was written. Why is it safe to simply run the command again?
check.a: The watermark moves only after a successful load, so the rerun extracts the same rows again. If a load had succeeded before a crash, the duplicates are removed in staging.

slides.title: Transform: clean and define inside the warehouse
slides.tldr: Staging removes duplicates by keeping the newest row per id. The mart settles the business definition once, in SQL, so every dashboard reads the same number.

blocks.body: Raw has duplicates, because the load appends and the extract can repeat rows. **Staging** keeps one row per order: the newest. The **mart** then applies the business rules once: only paid orders count, and the day is the order's day in New York time. This is where the three numbers from the first slide stop happening, because Finance, Marketing and the product team all read this one table.

blocks.code:
-- staging: the newest version of each order (duplicates removed)
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW staging.stg_orders AS
SELECT * EXCEPT (rn) FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM raw.raw_orders
)
WHERE rn = 1;

-- mart: the business definition is settled here, once
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW mart.mart_daily_sales AS
SELECT DATE(created_at, 'America/New_York') AS day,
       SUM(total_amount) AS revenue
FROM staging.stg_orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY day;

marks.tip: Number each id's rows from newest to oldest, then keep number 1. A re-loaded file just adds older copies that are dropped.
The day is the order's creation day in New York time, not UTC and not the last update. This ends the arguments about "month end".

blocks.title: What this settles
items: One definition: paid orders only, refunds excluded, day in New York time.
One place: every dashboard reads `mart_daily_sales`, not its own copy.
Rebuildable: change the rule, rerun the SQL, and the mart is recomputed from raw.
Keep the transform SQL in git; a tool like dbt can run it in order and test it too.
The transforms run on the warehouse's paid compute, and a view recomputes on every read. For a heavy mart, store it as a table rebuilt on a schedule.

check.q: What is the benefit of keeping the raw data untouched in ELT?
check.a: If a mistake turns up in a transformation rule, you can rebuild staging and the mart from raw, without going back to the source system.

slides.title: Batch or streaming: how fast do you need it?
slides.tldr: Batch moves data in one go at set times: simple and cheap. Streaming moves every event immediately: fast but complex. How much delay you can tolerate decides it.

blocks.body: A wholesale delivery arriving once a night by truck is **batch**: simple and cheap, but in the morning you're looking at last night's figures. Every packet arriving instantly on a conveyor belt is **streaming**: always current, but it needs machinery and someone watching it. Most reports are fine with "yesterday's data", so start with batch. You need a stream when you must react within minutes or seconds of an event, such as fraud detection.

blocks.caption: Two kinds of pipeline

columns.title: Batch
items: Data is hours or a day old
Simple, cheap, easy to rerun
If it fails, the whole batch reruns
Dashboards, monthly reports
columns.tip: Picks up data in one go at set times, such as every night or every hour.

columns.title: Streaming
items: Data is seconds to minutes old
Complex: ordering, late events, duplicates
Always running, needs monitoring
Fraud detection, live tracking
columns.tip: Each event enters the pipe as it happens and reaches the other end within seconds.

blocks.title: Questions that decide it
items: How old can the data be before it hurts? Hours or days means batch.
Must every event trigger immediate action (an alert, a block)? If so, streaming.
Can the team keep a pipeline running around the clock? If not, batch.

blocks.body: Start with batch. Only move to streaming once "we need it now" is proven.

use: Batch: daily sales reports, monthly accounts, ML training data
Streaming: fraud detection, live dashboards, search index sync
avoid: Installing Kafka just because it sounds "modern", where even minute-old data isn't needed

check.q: The daily sales report is needed at 9am. Batch or streaming, and why?
check.a: Batch. A few hours of staleness does no harm, and batch is simple, cheap and easy to rerun after a failure.

slides.title: Governance: owners, quality and a catalog
slides.tldr: Every dataset gets an owner, a written definition and quality checks, plus a catalog everyone can search. That settles "which number do I trust?".

blocks.body: Getting goods into the warehouse isn't enough; every shelf needs three things. An **owner**: who is responsible, and who you call when it's wrong. **Quality**: automatic checks, such as "revenue is never negative, and the data arrived before 6am". A **catalog**: a list of every dataset with its definition, so nobody quietly builds yet another copy. Together these three are data governance.

blocks.code:
dataset: mart_daily_sales
owner: team-finance-data          # who to tell when it's wrong
description: 'Daily paid sales, USD, day by New York time. Refunds excluded.'
freshness: 'Updated daily by 6am'
pii: false                        # no personal data
columns:
  day:     {type: date,   not_null: true, unique: true}
  revenue: {type: bigint, not_null: true, min: 0}

marks.tip: A team name, not a person's name. People move on; the team stays.
The promise is written down, so late data raises an alert instead of a guess.

blocks.code:
-- a check passes when its query returns zero rows; any row means failure
SELECT 'negative_revenue' AS failed_check, day
FROM mart_daily_sales WHERE revenue < 0
UNION ALL
SELECT 'duplicate_day', day
FROM mart_daily_sales GROUP BY day HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'stale_data', max(day)
FROM mart_daily_sales
HAVING max(day) < DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE('America/New_York'), INTERVAL 1 DAY);

marks.tip: In this convention a check means "look for bad rows"; zero rows means all is well.
The freshness check: if the latest day is older than yesterday, the pipeline is surely stuck.

blocks.title: Starting governance on a small team
items: One YAML or Markdown file in git per dataset: owner, definition, freshness.
Run quality checks as the last pipeline step; on failure, show a warning on the dashboard.
Mark columns holding personal data (`pii: true`) and restrict access.
The catalog can start as a wiki page; tools (DataHub, OpenMetadata) can come later.

check.q: A dashboard suddenly shows negative revenue. Which part of governance could have caught it earlier?
check.a: A quality check (a test that fails on `revenue < 0`). And with an owner assigned, they could have been notified the moment it failed.
